recall.q: Define pharmacology, and explain why knowledge of it matters to the Registered Nurse. Give four reasons.
a: Pharmacology is "the study of drugs, including their sources, nature, actions, effects in living systems, and uses".
Most nurses administer medication as part of their daily routine.
Nurses are legally and ethically responsible for the medications they administer, and for doing this safely.
Nurses provide education about medication to patients and whānau.
Nurses evaluate the outcome of medication use, including adverse effects.
With further training, nurse practitioners and nurse prescribers may prescribe and dispense medications.

recall.q: Define "medication". Name the six things a medication may be used to do, with an example of each from the lecture.
a: A medication is any substance used to prevent, diagnose, relieve, treat, or cure disease, or to affect the structure or function of the body.
PREVENT — minimise or avoid disease: Hepatitis B immunisation.
DIAGNOSE — help identify a disease: contrast media making areas show on X-ray or CT.
RELIEVE — reduce symptoms without fixing the cause: paracetamol for pain.
TREAT — manage or control but not cure: omeprazole reducing stomach acid to heal an ulcer.
CURE — completely eliminate: antifungal cream for a ringworm infection.
AFFECT STRUCTURE OR FUNCTION: the oral contraceptive pill preventing ovulation.

recall.q: Name the four branches of pharmacology covered in this course and define each in one line.
a: [[Pharmacokinetics]] — "what the body does to the drug"; four phases: absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion.
[[Pharmacodynamics]] — "what the drug does to the body", and how (mechanism of action); the interaction of drug molecules with receptors or other targets.
[[Pharmacotherapeutics]] — the application of medications to an individual patient; applying the science of PK and PD to prescribe and administer the most appropriate medication.
[[Toxicology]] — the study of the harmful effects of chemicals, including medications, on living organisms; includes misuse, adverse effects and poisoning.

recall.q: Three things a nurse must know before administering any medication to a patient. What are they?
a: How to safely administer the medication.
The intended effect (purpose) of the medication.
Possible adverse effects of the medication, including allergies.
The deck's framing: Registered Nurses must be well informed about each medication BEFORE administering it.

recall.q: Explain the difference between a contraindication and a precaution.
a: Contraindication: a situation in which a medication should NOT be used, because it may be harmful to the person.
Precaution: a warning that the medication should be used with special care because of a heightened risk of adverse effects.
Critically — with a precaution the medication MAY still be used, but only with careful monitoring or dose adjustment.

recall.q: What is a medication (drug) interaction? Name the four categories of thing a medication can interact with.
a: A reaction where the effect or activity of a medication is altered by another substance or condition.
Other medications.
Foods.
Complementary and alternative medicines.
Medical conditions.

recall.q: Distinguish the roles of PHARMAC and Medsafe.
a: [[PHARMAC — Te Pātaka Whaioranga]] is the government agency that decides which medications and medical products are FUNDED (subsidised) in Aotearoa NZ, within a fixed budget.
[[Medsafe]] is the New Zealand Medicines and Medical Devices Safety Authority — it REGULATES medicines and medical devices, making sure they are safe and high-quality.

recall.q: All medications are known by at least three names. Name and describe them, using paracetamol as the example.
a: [[Chemical name]] — precisely describes the atomic and molecular structure; long and impractical; used mainly by chemists. Paracetamol: 4-hydroxyacetanilide.
[[Generic name]] — assigned by the manufacturer with approval of the local drug regulating authority; becomes the official name; must be distinct in sound and spelling. Paracetamol.
[[Proprietary (brand) name]] — selected and copyrighted by the company that markets it; restricted to that company and that formulation. Panadol, Pamol, Pacimol, Paracare.

recall.q: Why are prescribers in Aotearoa NZ encouraged to prescribe generically, and what are the two exceptions?
a: Reduces the risk of error — many proprietary/brand names may exist for the same medication.
More cost-effective — the pharmacist will dispense subsidised medication brands wherever possible.
Exception 1: when the medication is a special modified-release form of the same generic drug.
Exception 2: when different brands of the same generic drug do not show [[Bioequivalence]] — the deck's example is epilepsy.

recall.q: Define bioequivalence, and explain its role in drug development.
a: Bioequivalence is when two medications containing the same active ingredient are administered at the same dose,
reach the bloodstream at a similar rate and extent,
AND lead to similar effects (beneficial or adverse) in the body.
A company developing a new branded version of a medicine already on the market must demonstrate bioequivalence to the original before it can be sold.
Some brands are more affordable for consumers and for the funder (PHARMAC).

recall.q: Name three generic-name suffixes taught in the lecture and the drug class each signals.
a: "-olol" — beta blockers, e.g. atenolol, propranolol, metoprolol.
"-statin" — cholesterol-lowering medication, e.g. atorvastatin.
"-cillin" — penicillin antibiotics, e.g. amoxicillin.

mcq.q: "What the body does to the drug" is the definition of:
mcq.why: The deck uses this exact phrasing for pharmacokinetics, and pairs it with the four phases: absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion. Pharmacodynamics is the mirror phrase — "what the drug does to the body".

mcq.q: A patient is prescribed omeprazole to reduce stomach acid so an ulcer can heal, although the underlying cause is not permanently fixed. Which purpose of a medication is this?
mcq.why: The deck uses this exact example for TREAT: "Omeprazole treats a stomach ulcer by reducing stomach acid and promoting healing, but does not permanently cure the underlying cause."

mcq.q: Which body decides whether a medicine is subsidised in Aotearoa New Zealand?
mcq.why: PHARMAC decides which medications and medical products are funded within a fixed budget. Medsafe regulates safety and quality — a different question.

mcq.q: "Panadol", "Pamol" and "Pacimol" are examples of which kind of name?
mcq.why: These are trade names selected and copyrighted by the companies that market paracetamol; the generic name is paracetamol and the chemical name is 4-hydroxyacetanilide.

mcq.q: A medication should NOT be used at all because it may harm this person. This is a:
mcq.why: A contraindication is an absolute — the medication should not be used. A precaution means it may still be used, but with careful monitoring or dose adjustment.

mcq.q: The suffix "-olol" (atenolol, propranolol, metoprolol) signals which drug class?
mcq.why: The deck lists three suffixes: -olol beta blockers, -statin cholesterol-lowering, -cillin penicillin antibiotics.

mcq.q: Rongoā Māori is placed under which branch of pharmacology in this course?
mcq.why: The deck states that indigenous medicines and practices "also sit under the umbrella of pharmacotherapeutics", and quotes the Ahuriri-Driscoll et al. (2008) definition of rongoā Māori.

recall.q: Name the three classification systems this course recommends, and give an example of each.
a: [[Clinical use classification]] — what the medication is prescribed for, e.g. analgesics for pain relief, bronchodilators to open airways.
[[Mechanism of action classification]] — how it produces its effect, e.g. proton pump inhibitors inhibit the H+/K+ proton pump in gastric parietal cells, blocking acid secretion.
[[Legal classification]] — according to NZ Medicines law, e.g. prescription, restricted, pharmacy-only, general sale.

recall.q: Aspirin is used as the lecture's example of one drug in several clinical-use classes. Name four classes it belongs to.
a: Analgesic (pain relief).
Antipyretic (reduce fever).
Anti-inflammatory (reduce inflammation).
Antithrombotic (prevent or treat blood clotting).

recall.q: List the four legal classifications of medicines under the Medicines Act 1981, what each means, and an example.
recall.src: Pharmacology Concepts (2) 2026 slide 10 · Legal & Ethical 2026 slide 8
a: [[Prescription medicine]] — supplied or administered under a prescription by an authorised, designated or delegated prescriber, or by standing order. Example: amoxicillin.
[[Restricted (pharmacist-only) medicine]] — sold or supplied only in a pharmacy or hospital; the pharmacist must explain it to the patient. Example: clotrimazole cream.
[[Pharmacy-only medicine]] — sold or supplied in a pharmacy or hospital, or a licensed shop in rural locations. Example: oxymetazoline (Otrivine) nasal spray.
[[General sales medicine]] — any other medicine not classified above; can be sold from any retail outlet. Example: paracetamol and ibuprofen.
The last three groups are what is commonly called "over the counter" (OTC).

recall.q: Name the two free New Zealand websites recommended as sources of medication information, and what each provides.
a: Medsafe (www.medsafe.govt.nz) — free; provides Data Sheets (suited to health professionals) and Consumer Medicine Information sheets (for health consumers).
The New Zealand Formulary (www.nzformulary.org) — free; adult section for over-18s and a child section for 0–18 years.
The NZF provides most key medication information, gives normal dosing, identifies whether a medication is PHARMAC-subsidised, and has an interactions checker.

recall.q: The deck lists four kinds of source to use WITH CAUTION. Name them and say why.
a: Other websites / any .com websites — often contain American terminology and information, e.g. Drugs.com.
News releases — watch out for clickbait; is the author a qualified health professional?
Artificial intelligence — "uses patterns rather than science", and includes sources such as Reddit.
Social media.

recall.q: What three things does the route of administration affect?
a: The rate of onset of action.
The magnitude of the body's response.
And for some routes, the location of the response.

recall.q: Name the five major groups of administration route, and explain the difference between a local and a systemic effect.
a: Oral (enteral — GI tract).
Parenteral (not through the GI tract).
Rectal.
Inhalation.
Topical.
[[Local effect]]: the effect occurs at the immediate site of administration.
[[Systemic effect]]: the medication must be absorbed before it enters the body's circulation, and is distributed to a location where it causes an effect.

recall.q: Give the advantages and disadvantages of the intravenous route.
a: ADVANTAGE: rapid effects — onset is immediate because the medication reaches circulation right away.
ADVANTAGE: a large volume of medication can be administered.
ADVANTAGE: reduced risk of tissue irritation, as the medication is immediately diluted within the blood volume.
DISADVANTAGE: can be dangerous — not easy to retrieve, stop or slow once administered.
DISADVANTAGE: may need hospitalisation; higher cost.
DISADVANTAGE: risk of infection and adverse effects.

recall.q: Compare the intramuscular and subcutaneous routes: absorption, one advantage and one disadvantage each.
a: IM: injected into muscle, absorbed into the blood vessels flowing through it; faster than oral unless it is a thick medication designed to absorb over time.
IM advantage: can be formulated for slower absorption (e.g. Depo-Provera for 13 weeks contraception); patient can self-administer (e.g. EpiPen).
IM disadvantage: risk of pain and nerve damage; slower onset/distribution; variable absorption.
SC: given beneath the skin into connective tissue or fat immediately under the dermis; faster than oral but less reliable, as local blood flow and tissue diffusion influence absorption.
SC advantage: slow absorption can provide a sustained effect (e.g. insulin); patient can self-medicate.
SC disadvantage: limited to non-irritating drugs; risk of irritation, pain and necrosis; slower onset; small volumes and doses only.

recall.q: Why can the lungs absorb medication so readily, and what physical form must an inhaled medication take?
a: The lungs have a large surface area for absorbing medications.
There are many capillaries adjacent to the alveolar membranes (air sacs), so medications can readily enter the bloodstream.
Inhaled medication must be in the form of gases or fine mists (aerosols) — e.g. asthma inhalers and nebulisers.

recall.q: Explain dissolution, and rank the oral formulations from fastest to slowest absorption.
a: Dissolution is where the drug goes into a solution. Solid forms must first disintegrate (break apart), then dissolve, to become available for absorption.
Faster dissolution = faster absorption. Liquid medications absorb fastest because they do not need to disintegrate.
Order: elixirs and syrups (fastest) → suspensions → powders → capsules → tablets → coated tablets, i.e. enteric-coated or sustained release (slowest).

recall.q: Give the four reasons an enteric coating is used.
a: Prevents decomposition of sensitive drugs by gastric secretions.
Prevents dilution of the drug.
Prevents nausea and vomiting induced by the drug's effect in the stomach.
Provides delayed action of the drug.
Mechanism: the coating prevents dissolution in the stomach; it dissolves in the intestine, and the medication is then absorbed.

recall.q: What are excipients, and name four kinds found in a tablet?
a: Excipients are inert chemicals in a formulation — e.g. fillers, colours, flavours, stabilisers.
The active medication may be only a very small fraction of the total tablet weight.

A tablet is compressed powdered medication that also contains: binders (adhesive to stick the powder together), disintegrators (to assist dissolution), lubricants (to make manufacturing easier), and fillers (for a convenient tablet size).

recall.q: Distinguish a hard capsule from a soft capsule (softgel).
a: Both encase the medication inside a gelatin shell.
Hard capsule: contains the drug as a solid (powder, granule). Can be opened and the contents emptied out if needed, e.g. some capsules in aged care.
Soft capsule (softgel): contains the drug as a liquid solution. Useful if fast action is required.

recall.q: Give the meaning of: prn, mane, nocte, od, bd, tds, qid, qqh, ac, pc, stat.
recall.src: Must Know: Medication & Prescription Abbreviations 01.26 (PDF) · Concepts (2) slide 77
a: prn — if necessary. mane — in the morning. nocte — at night.
od — once daily. bd / bid — twice a day. tds — three times a day.
qid — four times a day (four times in 24 hours). qqh, q4h — every four hours.
ac — before meals. pc — after meals. stat — immediately.

recall.q: Give the meaning of the route abbreviations PO, SL, SC, IM, IV, PR — and of NKA and NKDA.
recall.src: Must Know: Medication & Prescription Abbreviations 01.26 (PDF) · Concepts (2) slides 78 & 80
a: PO — orally. SL — sublingual (under the tongue). SC — subcut., subcutaneous.
IM — intramuscular. IV — intravenous. PR — rectally.
NKA — no known allergies. NKDA — no known drug allergies.

mcq.q: Under the Medicines Act 1981, paracetamol and ibuprofen are classified as:
mcq.why: The deck's legal classification table gives paracetamol and ibuprofen as the general-sales examples — any other medicine not classified above, sellable from any retail outlet.

mcq.q: Which oral formulation is absorbed FASTEST?
mcq.why: The deck's rate-of-absorption table runs elixirs and syrups (fastest) → suspensions → powders → capsules → tablets → coated tablets (slowest). Liquids do not need to disintegrate first.

mcq.q: GTN spray for angina is given under the tongue so it enters the bloodstream directly and acts very quickly. This route is:
mcq.why: Sublingual = under the tongue (GTN spray is the deck's own example). Buccal is through the mucosal lining of the cheek — the deck's example there is nicotine gum.

mcq.q: A tuberculosis vaccination or an allergy antigen test is injected just under the epidermis. This route is:
mcq.why: Intradermal is injected into the dermis, just under the epidermis; the deck names antigen (allergy) testing and TB vaccination as the examples.

mcq.q: Which parenteral route bypasses the blood–brain barrier by injecting directly into the spinal subarachnoid space?
mcq.why: Intrathecal is injection directly into the spinal subarachnoid space, bypassing the blood–brain barrier, e.g. spinal anaesthesia. Epidural is into the epidural space of the spinal canal.

mcq.q: "tds" on a medication chart means:
mcq.why: From the Must Know Abbreviations table: tds = three times a day. Twice a day is bd/bid; immediately is stat.

mcq.q: Which is NOT one of the four reasons the lecture gives for using an enteric coating?
options: Prevents decomposition of sensitive drugs by gastric secretions
Prevents nausea and vomiting induced by the drug in the stomach
Provides delayed action of the drug
Increases the total dose absorbed above 100%
mcq.why: The four reasons are: prevent decomposition by gastric secretions, prevent dilution of the drug, prevent drug-induced nausea and vomiting, and provide delayed action. A coating cannot raise bioavailability above the dose given.

mcq.q: Which source does the lecture explicitly warn against because it "uses patterns rather than science"?
mcq.why: The "sources to use with caution" slide names AI directly with that wording, alongside .com websites, news releases and social media. Intranet policies, pharmacy, manufacturer inserts, current textbooks and dated journal articles are listed as APPROPRIATE sources.

recall.q: State the main medication calculation formula, say what each term means, and list the three kinds of medication it works for.
a: Formula: (what you WANT ÷ what you have GOT) × VOLUME = the dosage amount to administer.
What you want = "prescribed", "charted", "ordered", "is to be given".
What you have got = "in stock", "on hand", or "you have".
Volume = the volume or unit the stock strength comes in (1 tablet, 5 mL, 2 mL).
Works for: oral tablets and capsules; oral liquids (elixir, syrup, suspension); injected medicines including SC, IM and direct IV.
Some sources write the volume over 1 — that is also accurate, since any number divided by 1 is itself.

recall.q: List the five steps of the Medication Calculation Checklist taught in this course.
a: No distractions.
Are the units the same?
Formula.
Does the answer look correct?
Double check.

recall.q: A patient has been prescribed digoxin 0.25 mg. You have tablets of 62.5 mcg. How many tablets should you give? Show the conversion.
a: mg ≠ mcg, so convert first: 0.25 mg × 1000 = 250 mcg prescribed.
250 mcg ÷ 62.5 mcg × 1 tablet.
= 4 tablets.

recall.q: A child is prescribed paracetamol 250 mg. The suspension contains 200 mg/5 mL. What volume do you give?
a: Units already match (mg and mg), so no conversion needed.

recall.q: Te Atawhai is prescribed furosemide 0.1 g IM. You have furosemide 20 mg/2 mL. What volume is required?
a: Convert: 0.1 g × 1000 = 100 mg furosemide.
100 mg ÷ 20 mg × 2 mL.

recall.q: State the body-weight dosing formula, and use it: ampicillin 10 mg/kg every 6 hours for Wei, who weighs 30 kg. What is the single dose?
a: Formula: dose per kg (mg/kg) × body weight (kg) = administered dose.
Read the "/" as "per" — 10 mg/kg means 10 milligrams per kilogram.
10 mg/kg × 30 kg = 300 mg. The single dose for Wei is 300 mg.

recall.q: Naveen weighs 40 kg and is prescribed prednisone 1 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses. You have 5 mg tablets. How many tablets per dose? Show all three steps.
a: Step 1 — daily dose: 40 kg × 1 mg/kg/day = 40 mg per day.
Step 2 — single dose: 40 mg ÷ 2 doses = 20 mg per dose.
Step 3 — oral tablet formula: 20 mg ÷ 5 mg × 1 tablet = 4 tablets.

recall.q: State the IV drip-rate formula and explain the difference between drop factor and drip rate.
a: Drip rate (drops/min) = [volume to be given (mL) × drop factor] ÷ [time (hours) × 60 (minutes)].
[[Drop factor]] = drops/mL (gtt/mL) — how BIG the drops are, i.e. how many drops make 1 mL. It is fixed by the type of giving set and you are always given it.
[[Drip rate]] = drops/min (gtt/min) — how FAST the drops are delivered. It is adjustable and is what the nurse calculates.
You can tell drip rate is about speed because it is per minute, not per mL.

recall.q: Tania is prescribed Sodium Chloride 0.9% 1000 mL over 12 hours. The giving set delivers 60 drops per mL. What rate should the nurse set?
a: Top: 1000 mL × 60 drops/mL = 60,000 drops.
Bottom: 12 hr × 60 = 720 minutes.
Round DOWN (.4 or lower) → 83 drops per minute.

recall.q: Mr Willis is prescribed Sodium Chloride 0.9% 1 L over 5 hours, drop factor 20 gtt/mL. What rate should be set?
a: Convert first: 1 L = 1000 mL (the formula requires mL).
Top: 1000 mL × 20 drops/mL = 20,000 drops. Bottom: 5 hr × 60 = 300 minutes.
Round UP (.5 or higher) → 67 drops per minute.

recall.q: Explain the order-of-operations trap in the drip-rate calculation, using the deck's own numbers.
a: You must complete unit conversions and the top/bottom multiplications FIRST, before dividing.
Typing 1000 × 60 ÷ 12 × 60 into a calculator returns 300,000 drops/min — impossible.
That happens because the calculator did 60 ÷ 12 first.
Correct order: 1000 × 60 = 60,000 on top; 12 × 60 = 720 on the bottom; then 60,000 ÷ 720 = 83.33 drops/min.

recall.q: What does the ratio 1:1000 mean for adrenaline, and how is it derived?
a: 1:1000 means 1 mg in 1 mL.
The 1:1000 number literally means 1 g in 1000 mL.
Through unit conversion, 1 g × 1000 = 1000 mg, so 1000 mg:1000 mL.
Simplify by dividing both sides by 1000 → 1 mg:1 mL.
Modern packaging shows the ratio AND the mg/mL concentration; use the mg/mL for calculations.

recall.q: Mrs Dell needs adrenaline 0.7 mg. The ampoule contains 1:1000 (1 mg/1 mL). How much is administered?
a: Recognise 1:1000 as 1 mg/1 mL, then use the standard formula.
0.7 mg ÷ 1 mg × 1 mL.
= 0.7 mL administered.

recall.q: Mr Singh is prescribed 4 mg of morphine. Morphine comes in 1 mL ampoules of 5 mg/mL. You dilute one ampoule with 9 mL of sterile water. How many mL do you administer?
a: Do the ADDITION first: 1 mL ampoule + 9 mL water = 10 mL total volume in the syringe.
The syringe now holds 5 mg in 10 mL.
4 mg ÷ 5 mg × 10 mL = 8 mL.

recall.q: Explain the order-of-operations trap in a syringe dilution, using the deck's XD example.
a: If a calculation includes addition, you must do the addition FIRST, before putting numbers into the formula.
Typing 3 ÷ 10 × 9 + 1 returns 3.7 mL — an overdose — because the calculator adds the 1 last.
Correct order: 9 mL + 1 mL = 10 mL volume; then 3 mg ÷ 10 mg × 10 mL = 3 mL.

recall.q: 5-year-old Sophie is charted amoxicillin 400 mg. The reconstituted 150 mL bottle has a concentration of 250 mg/5 mL. What volume do you give — and what is the trap?
a: Want 400 mg; got 250 mg; volume 5 mL — NOT 150 mL.
400 mg ÷ 250 mg × 5 mL = 8 mL.
The trap: using the whole bottle volume (150 mL) gives 400 ÷ 250 × 150 = 240 mL, which the checklist should stop you on as a very unusual dose.
The formula can work from the whole bottle, but only with an extra step (250 mg × 30 = 7500 mg in the bottle → 400 ÷ 7500 × 150 = 8 mL) — harder, and it risks error.

recall.q: State the two rounding rules for this course.
a: Do NOT round medication volumes (mL) or tablet numbers.
DO round IV drip rates, because the nurse is counting whole drops and cannot count less than one.
For drip rates: .4 or lower rounds DOWN; .5 or higher rounds UP. E.g. 66.666 drops → 67 drops/min.

recall.q: What is a "red herring" in a calculation question? Give the deck's two examples.
a: A name or number in the question that does not relate to your calculation formula.
Example: the concentration of the IV fluid (Dextrose 5%) when you are working out a drip rate.
Example: the frequency (tds) when you are working out how many tablets to give in a SINGLE dose.

mcq.q: You are prescribed 1 g of paracetamol and have 500 mg capsules. Before using the formula you must:
options: Convert 1 g to 1000 mg so the units match
mcq.why: The unit of medication must be the same on the top and bottom of the formula. 1 g × 1000 = 1000 mg; then 1000 ÷ 500 × 1 capsule = 2 capsules.

mcq.q: The drop factor of a giving set is:
options: How fast the drops fall, calculated by the nurse
How big the drops are, fixed by the manufacturer
The total volume to be infused
The time the infusion will take
mcq.why: Drop factor = drops/mL — the SIZE of the drops, a fixed number set by the type of giving set. The nurse never calculates it. The drip rate (drops/min) is the speed, and that IS calculated.

mcq.q: An IV drip rate calculates to 27.77 drops/min. What rate do you set?
mcq.why: IV drip rates are rounded: .5 or higher rounds UP, so 27.77 → 28 drops/min. This is the deck's worked example 15 (Kohatu, Dextrose 5% 500 mL over 6 hours, drop factor 20).

mcq.q: Adrenaline for injection 1:1000 means:
mcq.why: 1:1000 literally means 1 g in 1000 mL; converting gives 1000 mg:1000 mL, which simplifies to 1 mg in 1 mL. The deck calls this "the most important thing about ratios at this level".

mcq.q: Which of these should you NOT round?
options: An IV drip rate of 83.33 drops/min
An IV drip rate of 66.66 drops/min
An IV drip rate of 55.55 drops/min
mcq.why: Do not round medication volumes or tablet numbers — 6.25 mL is given as 6.25 mL. Drip rates ARE rounded, because you cannot count a fraction of a drop.

mcq.q: You dilute a 1 mL ampoule of morphine 5 mg/mL with 9 mL of sterile water. The concentration in the syringe is now:
mcq.why: The amount of drug is unchanged — 5 mg went in. The volume is 1 mL + 9 mL = 10 mL. So the syringe holds 5 mg in 10 mL.

mcq.q: How many resits are available for the Medication Calculations Test in Semester 2, and what score is required?
mcq.why: The Student Guide: Semester 2 allows up to 3 resits, and 100% competency is required. Fail after the third attempt and you fail the course.

mcq.q: Mele is prescribed pethidine 75 mg IM. Ampoules contain 100 mg in 2 mL. What volume do you draw up?
mcq.why: 75 mg ÷ 100 mg × 2 mL = 1.5 mL. This is the deck's worked example 6.

recall.q: Define pharmacokinetics and name its four processes, describing each in one line.
a: Pharmacokinetics is "what the body does to the drug" — the passage of a drug through the body.
Absorption — the entry of a drug into the bloodstream.
Distribution — the movement of a drug between the blood and body tissues.
Metabolism — the modification of a drug (usually by the liver).
Excretion — the removal of a drug (and its metabolites) from the body.

recall.q: Define absorption. Which route does not require it, and why?
a: [[Absorption]] is the process by which an unchanged drug reaches the bloodstream (systemic circulation) after administration and dissolution.
Absorption plays a key role in every method of drug administration EXCEPT the intravenous route.
IV medications enter the bloodstream directly and do not need to be absorbed from the site they are given.

recall.q: Name the seven factors affecting absorption listed in the lecture.
a: Route of administration of the drug.
Blood flow at the site of absorption.
Nature of the membrane.
Medication formulation.
Solubility of the drug.
GI tract status.
pH of the small intestine.

recall.q: Explain how the nature of the membrane affects absorption, with an example of each property.
a: SURFACE AREA: greater surface area = greater absorption. The small intestine has a very large surface area (villi); the oral mucosa has a small surface area.
THICKNESS: thinner membrane = faster absorption. A single layer, e.g. the epithelium of the small intestine, gives rapid absorption.
A multi-layered membrane, e.g. the thick skin on the palms of the hands, gives slower absorption.

recall.q: Why are lipid-soluble drugs absorbed more rapidly than water-soluble drugs?
a: [[Solubility]] is the ability of a substance to be dissolved into a solution.
Cell membranes are composed of a lipid bilayer.
So lipid-soluble drugs are rapidly absorbed, and water-soluble drugs are poorly absorbed.

recall.q: Describe how blood flow affects absorption, and give a disease example.
a: Absorption into the bloodstream depends on the blood flow at the site.
High blood supply → faster absorption, e.g. sublingual.
Low blood supply → slower absorption, e.g. topical.
Blood flow can be impacted by disease state — poor peripheral circulation in shock can significantly reduce absorption of intramuscular injections.

recall.q: Give two examples of food affecting drug absorption from the lecture.
a: Dairy (milk, yoghurt) can bind to certain antibiotics (tetracyclines) and prevent absorption.
Tannins in tea and coffee bind to iron, stopping its absorption.

recall.q: Define bioavailability. What is it for an IV medication, and what two things determine it for an oral one?
a: [[Bioavailability]] is how much of the drug actually reaches the bloodstream.
For intravenous medications, bioavailability = 100%.
For oral medications it depends on how much of the drug is absorbed in the GI tract,
and how much of the drug "escapes" being broken down by the liver.

recall.q: Explain the hepatic first-pass effect, and work through the lecture's 100 mg example to give the bioavailability.
a: [[Hepatic first-pass effect]]: medicine taken orally is absorbed from the gut, then takes a "first pass" through the liver before it can reach the rest of the body.
The liver acts like a filter, breaking down part of the drug as it passes through, so only a portion of the original dose reaches the bloodstream unchanged.
You take a tablet with 100 mg of drug. 20 mg is not absorbed in the gut. 80 mg reaches the liver.
The liver breaks down 60 mg on the first pass. So only 20 mg gets into the bloodstream to have an effect.
This drug therefore has a bioavailability of 20%.

recall.q: Explain plasma protein binding and why it matters, including what happens when two drugs compete.
a: Many drugs bind reversibly to plasma proteins, mainly albumin.
Only FREE (unbound) drug can move from the bloodstream into tissues to produce a pharmacological effect.
Drugs vary in [[Affinity (protein binding)]] — some are highly protein-bound (warfarin at 99%), leaving very little free drug available.
Binding is dynamic: as free drug is removed from circulation (by distribution, metabolism or excretion), more free drug is released to replace what is lost.
Two drugs can compete for the same binding site, which may increase the amount of free drug and its effect.

recall.q: Compare the blood–brain barrier and the placental barrier.
a: [[Blood–brain barrier]]: a protective barrier that limits entry of substances into the brain, while allowing essential molecules like oxygen and glucose through.
Only small, lipid-soluble drugs pass effectively — brain capillary cells are tightly joined with a thick basement membrane, and brain cell membranes have a lipid bilayer.
The BBB may be disrupted in illness, e.g. meningitis.
[[Placental barrier]]: separates maternal and foetal blood vessels, but is NON-SELECTIVE — it allows many different drugs to cross.
Lipid-soluble drugs cross the placenta easily.

recall.q: Name three tissues where drugs get concentrated, with the lecture's example for each.
a: Bone tissue — e.g. tetracycline, which can discolour children's teeth.
Adipose tissue — lipid-soluble drugs, e.g. diazepam.
Thyroid gland — medications containing iodine.

mcq.q: Which route of administration does NOT require absorption?
mcq.why: IV medications enter the bloodstream directly and do not need to be absorbed from the site they are given. Every other route requires absorption.

mcq.q: A 100 mg oral tablet: 20 mg is not absorbed, 80 mg reaches the liver, and the liver breaks down 60 mg on the first pass. The bioavailability is:
mcq.why: Only 20 mg gets into the bloodstream to have effect, out of the 100 mg dose — a bioavailability of 20%. This is the deck's own worked example.

mcq.q: Only which fraction of a drug can leave the bloodstream and produce an effect?
mcq.why: Only free (unbound) drug can move from the bloodstream into tissues to produce a pharmacological effect. Warfarin is about 99% protein-bound, so very little free drug is available.

mcq.q: The placental barrier is best described as:
options: Highly selective — very few drugs cross
Non-selective — many drugs cross, and lipid-soluble drugs cross easily
mcq.why: The lecture describes the placenta as a non-selective barrier that allows many different drugs to cross, with lipid-soluble drugs crossing easily. The blood–brain barrier is the selective one.

mcq.q: Where does most absorption of an oral medication occur?
mcq.why: The small intestine is the main site of absorption — it has a very large surface area and abundant blood vessels. Absorption in the stomach is low (thick mucus, tight junctions, small surface area).

mcq.q: Movement of a drug across a membrane against its concentration gradient, using ATP, is:
mcq.why: Active transport is movement against the concentration gradient using energy (ATP). Passive transport is movement along the gradient without energy.

mcq.q: Which tissue does the lecture pair with tetracycline, as a site where the drug becomes concentrated?
mcq.why: Bone tissue — the deck notes tetracycline can discolour children's teeth. Adipose is paired with lipid-soluble drugs like diazepam, and the thyroid with iodine-containing medications.

recall.q: Define drug metabolism. Name the main organ and three others, and state the three properties a metabolite usually has.
a: [[Metabolism (biotransformation)]] is the biological transformation of a drug into an inactive and water-soluble compound which can be excreted, almost always carried out by enzymes.
Main organ: the liver. Also the kidneys, the lungs and the intestinal mucosa.
Metabolites are usually more water-soluble (easier to excrete), less active or inactive, and usually less toxic.
Two exceptions the deck flags: some drugs are ACTIVATED by the liver, and a few can be converted into TOXIC metabolites.

recall.q: Name the five sources of inter-individual variation in drug metabolism.
a: Genetics.
Environmental factors.
Disease states.
Age and gender.
Hormonal changes.

recall.q: Contrast enzyme inducers and enzyme inhibitors, including the effect on dosing.
a: [[Enzyme inducer]]: activates liver enzymes → accelerates metabolism → decreases the amount of drug that reaches the bloodstream.
So a higher dose may be needed to achieve the intended effect.
[[Enzyme inhibitor]]: inhibits liver enzymes → slows down metabolism → increases the amount of drug that reaches the bloodstream.
So toxicity may increase.
Environmental factors that do this include diet, co-administered drugs, alcohol and smoking.

recall.q: Explain how heart failure and cirrhosis each affect drug metabolism, and what this means for care.
a: Heart failure: decreased liver perfusion and oxygenation → reduced liver enzyme activity → reduced drug metabolism → more active drug in the blood.
Cirrhosis (liver scarring): reduced enzyme activity → reduced clearance → more active drug in the blood.
Implications: reduced doses, close monitoring of therapeutic and toxic drug effects, and consideration of contraindications and alternative medications.

recall.q: Name the main medication routes that AVOID hepatic first-pass metabolism.
a: Sublingual and buccal.
Intravenous (IV).
Intramuscular (IM).
Subcutaneous (SC).
Inhalation.
Intranasal.
Transdermal (patches).
Rectal.
The reason: they do not travel through the portal vein after being absorbed.

recall.q: List the routes of drug excretion, naming the main organ.
a: Kidneys (main organ) → urine.
Liver → bile → faeces.
Lungs → expired air (e.g. the alcohol breath test).
Bowel.
Breast milk.
Sweat and saliva (minimal).

recall.q: Name the four factors affecting drug excretion by the kidneys.
a: Water-soluble drugs — better excretion; the kidneys are the main organ for eliminating water-soluble substances.
Lipid-soluble drugs — poorly excreted, because they are reabsorbed.
Protein-bound drugs — not excreted, so they circulate longer.
Impaired renal function → reduced excretion of drugs. Important in renal failure, neonates and the elderly.

recall.q: Distinguish excretion, elimination and clearance.
a: [[Excretion]] is the physical removal of waste products or unchanged drugs from the body.
[[Elimination]] is the process of the body removing a drug from the bloodstream. Elimination = metabolism + excretion.
So a drug is eliminated when it is metabolised into an inactive metabolite, even before it is physically excreted in the urine.
[[Clearance]] is a measure of the rate (speed) of elimination of a drug from the bloodstream — and it is irreversible; the drug leaves and cannot come back.

recall.q: Compare hepatic clearance and renal clearance.
a: [[Hepatic clearance]] occurs in the liver, through metabolism (the major process, via enzymes) and excretion (a minor process, in the bile).
If hepatic clearance is high, all of the drug going through the liver is metabolised (and vice versa).
[[Renal clearance]] occurs in the kidneys, through excretion into the urine. Some reabsorption occurs, where the drug moves back into the plasma.

recall.q: Define half-life and steady state, and state how long steady state takes to reach.
a: [[Half-life]] is the time taken for the plasma drug concentration to fall (decrease) by one-half. Also called the elimination half-life; it tells us how fast the drug leaves the body.
[[Steady state]] is where the rate of drug in = the rate of drug out, i.e. drug administration rate = drug elimination rate.
For most medications given at a constant dosing interval, it takes about 3–5 half-lives to reach steady state.

recall.q: What is a dosing regimen for, and what is it individualised against?
a: Pharmacokinetic processes (ADME) affect how much drug reaches the bloodstream and how long it acts for.
[[Dosing regimen]]s maintain plasma drug concentrations within the [[Therapeutic range]].
They are individualised for each medication (during clinical trials) and for each patient — e.g. age, interactions, liver function, kidney function.
Example: amoxicillin, take 500 mg orally every 8 hours for 5 days.

recall.q: Define the therapeutic range, and explain therapeutic drug monitoring including what is measured.
a: The [[Therapeutic range]] is the plasma concentration range within which a drug produces its desired therapeutic effect (efficacy) without causing toxicity (safety).
[[Therapeutic drug monitoring]] is used for drugs with a narrow therapeutic range, e.g. warfarin, an anticoagulant used to reduce the risk of stroke.
Points measured: peak concentration and trough concentration.
It ensures the concentration of drug in the blood stays within the safe and effective range.

recall.q: Summarise the pharmacokinetics of paracetamol under all four ADME headings.
a: ABSORPTION: rapidly absorbed following oral administration; absorption can be delayed by agents that slow gastric emptying, e.g. food.
DISTRIBUTION: after absorption, distributed widely throughout body tissues; only a small proportion is protein-bound, so many drug molecules are available to act.
METABOLISM: primarily metabolised in the liver. A small amount is converted to a hepatotoxic metabolite, which can accumulate after overdose and, if untreated, cause liver damage.
EXCRETION: metabolites are excreted in the urine. The elimination half-life varies from 1–3 hours.
Most of each dose is excreted in the urine within 24 hours.

mcq.q: Elimination is best defined as:
mcq.why: The deck states elimination = metabolism + excretion. A drug is eliminated when it is metabolised into an inactive metabolite, even before it is physically excreted in the urine.

mcq.q: A patient starts a medication that is a potent enzyme INDUCER alongside their regular drug. The likely consequence for the regular drug is:
options: Decreased plasma levels, possibly requiring a higher dose
mcq.why: Enzyme inducers activate liver enzymes → accelerate metabolism → decrease the amount of drug reaching the bloodstream, so a higher dose may be needed. Inhibitors do the opposite and may increase toxicity.

mcq.q: Roughly how many half-lives does it take for most drugs at a constant dosing interval to reach steady state?
mcq.why: The deck: "For most medications given at a constant dosing interval, it takes about 3-5 half-lives to reach steady state."

mcq.q: Which of these routes does NOT avoid hepatic first-pass metabolism?
mcq.why: The oral route is precisely the one that takes the first pass through the liver, because absorbed drug travels via the portal vein. Sublingual/buccal, IV, IM, SC, inhalation, intranasal, transdermal and rectal all avoid it.

mcq.q: Half-life is defined as the time taken for:
options: The whole drug to leave the body
The plasma drug concentration to fall by one-half
Half the dose to be absorbed
mcq.why: Half-life is the time for the plasma drug concentration to decrease by one-half. The Code of Conduct deck note makes the same point: it is not how long the whole drug stays in your system.

mcq.q: Which kind of drug is POORLY excreted by the kidneys because it is reabsorbed?
mcq.why: Lipid-soluble drugs are poorly excreted because they are reabsorbed. The kidneys are the main organ for eliminating water-soluble substances. Protein-bound drugs are not excreted while bound and circulate longer.

mcq.q: A higher-than-maintenance first dose, used to reach therapeutic plasma concentrations quickly, is a:
mcq.why: A loading dose is particularly important for drugs with a long half-life, where regular dosing alone would take a prolonged period to reach an effective range.

mcq.q: Paracetamol's elimination half-life is given in the Medsafe data sheet as:
mcq.why: The deck quotes the Medsafe Pacimol data sheet: the elimination half-life varies from 1–3 hours, and most of each dose is excreted in the urine within 24 hours.

recall.q: Define pharmacodynamics and state the four questions it asks.
a: [[Pharmacodynamics]] is the study of drug–target interactions, mechanisms of action, and the resulting biological effects — "what the drug does to the body".
Where exactly does the drug act?
How does the drug act?
What changes in function will it cause?
What happens to drug effects with time?

recall.q: Distinguish selectivity from specificity, and give the lecture's selectivity example.
a: [[Selectivity]] = the number of TARGETS a drug interacts with. High selectivity → preference for one target; low → binds multiple targets.
[[Specificity]] = the number of EFFECTS a drug produces. High specificity → one main effect; low → multiple effects at multiple sites or tissues.
No drug is completely specific; most cause more than one effect.
Example: salbutamol is selective for beta-2 receptors in lung tissue, especially when inhaled, and has little effect on beta receptors in the heart.

recall.q: Define affinity, efficacy and potency.
a: [[Affinity]]: how strongly the drug binds to its target. High affinity → binds strongly and tends to stay bound; low affinity → binds weakly and may detach easily.

[[Efficacy]]: the ability of a drug to activate its target and produce a biological response. Maximal efficacy is the greatest possible response even if the dose is increased further — the upper limit of the drug's action.
[[Potency]]: the amount of drug required to produce a given effect. High potency = the same effect at a lower dose; low potency = a higher dose needed for that same effect.

recall.q: Name the four main regulatory proteins drugs act on, with the lecture's drug example for each.
a: [[Transporter]] — fluoxetine, an SSRI, blocks the serotonin transporter so more serotonin stays available to improve mood.
[[Ion channel]] — amlodipine blocks the movement of calcium ions into muscle cells, relaxing blood vessels and slowing the heartbeat.
[[Enzyme (as a drug target)]] — ibuprofen inhibits COX enzymes to partially block the pathway that causes pain, fever and inflammation.
[[Receptor]] — large protein molecules, usually on the cell membrane, that a drug binds to, triggering a signal that changes cell function.

recall.q: Explain the difference between an agonist and an antagonist using the lock-and-key analogy.
a: [[Agonist]]: the drug binds to AND activates a receptor, producing the same effect as the endogenous chemical substance.
An agonist has affinity for a receptor AND efficacy — the key fits the lock and opens the door. Example: salbutamol binds beta receptors to relax the airways.
[[Antagonist]]: the drug binds to the receptor and blocks access of the endogenous substance, but does not elicit a response.
An antagonist has affinity for a receptor BUT NO efficacy — the key fits the lock, but the door will not open. Example: metoprolol, a beta blocker, prevents binding to beta receptors.

recall.q: Explain receptor up-regulation and down-regulation, with the lecture's clinical example of each.
a: Cells can change how many receptors they have on their surface.
[[Upregulation]]: more receptors → the cell is more sensitive. Often occurs when receptors are repeatedly BLOCKED.
If the drug is suddenly stopped the body may become over-responsive to endogenous signals — e.g. rebound hypertension after stopping long-term beta-blockers.
[[Downregulation]]: fewer receptors → the cell is less responsive. Often occurs when receptors are repeatedly STIMULATED.
E.g. chronic opioid use overstimulates opioid receptors, leading to downregulation and desensitisation, so patients respond less to the same dose over time (tolerance).

recall.q: What are non-specific drug actions? Give two examples.
a: Some drugs do not rely on specific targets; instead they act through chemical reactions, physical properties, or changes in the environment.
Activated charcoal — absorbs toxins from the gut, which are then excreted.
Calcium carbonate chews (e.g. Quick-Eze) — neutralise stomach acid.

recall.q: Describe the dose-response relationship.
a: The [[Dose-response relationship]] describes how the size of a drug's effect changes as the dose of the drug changes.
At low doses, there may be little or no effect.
As the dose increases, the response increases.
Eventually the response reaches maximal efficacy, where giving more drug will not increase the effect.

recall.q: Define the therapeutic range in pharmacodynamic terms, including MEC and MTC.
a: The therapeutic range is a measure of the safety margin of the drug — the range between efficacy and toxicity.
A wider range = a safer drug.
[[Minimum effective concentration (MEC)]]: the lowest plasma concentration that produces a therapeutic (beneficial) effect.
[[Minimum toxic concentration (MTC)]]: the lowest plasma concentration at which toxic (harmful) effects begin.

recall.q: Explain how pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics are linked.
a: The rate (timing) and extent (amount) of the drug response depends heavily on pharmacokinetics — what the body does to the drug.
Pharmacokinetics determines how much drug reaches the site of action.
That in turn impacts the onset, intensity and duration of the pharmacodynamic effect.
Pharmacokinetic concepts help us understand why drug responses change over time.

recall.q: Define an adverse effect and distinguish it from an adverse drug event.
a: An adverse effect is a "harmful effect suspected to be caused by a medicine or vaccine".
All medications cause adverse effects in some people, but most people take medicines without suffering any serious adverse effects.
They range from mild (e.g. nausea) to serious (e.g. liver injury); some can be predicted, others occur unexpectedly, e.g. severe allergy.
Also known as adverse drug reactions, side effects or undesirable effects — "adverse effect" is the preferred term.
An [[Adverse drug event]] is an injury related to the drug but not always DUE to the drug — e.g. errors in prescribing, dispensing or administration (often human error).

recall.q: List the six PERSON-related risk factors for adverse effects.
a: Age — neonates or older persons.
Sex — female sex (XX chromosomes at birth) appear to be more susceptible.
Organ health — kidney or liver disease.
Genetic factors — e.g. certain genes may predispose to allergy.
History of prior adverse effects from drugs.
Polypharmacy (taking five drugs or more).

recall.q: List the five DRUG-related risk factors for adverse effects.
a: Chemical characteristics — e.g. drugs with large molecules can trigger an immune reaction, or drugs with low selectivity act on multiple receptors.
Drug class — e.g. anticoagulants like aspirin have higher bleeding risk.
Route of administration — e.g. the oral route has lower allergy risk than the IV route.
Dose — higher doses increase risk.
Duration and frequency — longer or more frequent use increases risk.

recall.q: Give the lecture's two examples of pharmacodynamic drug–drug interactions and explain each mechanism.
a: Pharmacodynamic drug interactions occur when one drug (including complementary therapies) directly alters the effect of another drug.
Warfarin and aspirin → increased risk of bleeding, as both drugs inhibit clotting in different ways (an additive effect).

Metoprolol and salbutamol → reduced effect of salbutamol in the lungs when managing asthma, because salbutamol acts on beta receptors as an agonist, but metoprolol blocks beta receptors as an antagonist.

recall.q: What is CARM, who may report to it, and why does it matter?
a: [[CARM]] is the Centre for Adverse Reactions Monitoring.
It is important to document ALL adverse effects — patients may need alerts.
Reports of suspected adverse reactions are submitted to an online database; CARM further assesses serious and fatal events.
Who can report: health professionals, patients and whānau.

mcq.q: Selectivity refers to the number of ___ ; specificity refers to the number of ___ .
mcq.why: The deck has a slide dedicated to this pair: "Specificity = number of effects. Selectivity = number of targets."

mcq.q: A drug that has affinity for a receptor BUT NO efficacy is:
mcq.why: The key fits the lock, but the door will not open. An agonist has affinity AND efficacy; an antagonist blocks access of the endogenous substance without eliciting a response.

mcq.q: Amlodipine relaxes blood vessels by blocking the movement of calcium into muscle cells. Its drug target is:
mcq.why: Ion channels are membrane pores that let ions move across an electrochemical gradient; amlodipine is the deck's own ion-channel example.

mcq.q: Ibuprofen inhibits COX to block the pathway causing pain, fever and inflammation. Its drug target is:
mcq.why: Enzymes are biological catalysts; most drugs acting on enzymes inhibit them, and ibuprofen inhibiting COX is the deck's enzyme example.

mcq.q: Rebound hypertension after suddenly stopping a long-term beta-blocker is explained by:
mcq.why: Repeatedly blocking receptors causes upregulation — more receptors, greater sensitivity. Stopping the drug suddenly leaves the body over-responsive to endogenous signals.

mcq.q: Chronic opioid use leads to needing more drug for the same effect. This tolerance is caused by:
mcq.why: Repeated stimulation of receptors causes downregulation — fewer receptors, less responsive — so patients respond less to the same dose over time.

mcq.q: A drug that achieves the same effect at a LOWER dose than another is said to have higher:
mcq.why: Potency is the amount of drug required to produce a given effect. Efficacy is the size of the maximal response, which is a different question.

mcq.q: A patient is given the wrong dose because of a transcription error and is injured. This is best described as:
mcq.why: An adverse drug event is an injury related to the drug but not always due to the drug — including errors in prescribing, dispensing or administration. An adverse effect is caused by the medicine itself.

mcq.q: Which pair of drugs does the lecture use to illustrate an ADDITIVE pharmacodynamic interaction?
mcq.why: Warfarin and aspirin → increased bleeding risk, as both inhibit clotting in different ways (additive). Metoprolol and salbutamol is the OPPOSING example — agonist versus antagonist at beta receptors.

topics.name: Administration — 8 Rights + 2 Checks
topics.chapters: Module 5 · Med Admin (1) · Potter & Perry ch. 19

recall.q: Name the five authorised prescribers and the designated prescribers in Aotearoa NZ.
recall.src: Med Admin (1) 2026 slide 4 · Legal & Ethical 2026 slide 7
a: AUTHORISED prescribers: doctors, nurse practitioners, dentists, optometrists, registered midwives.
DESIGNATED prescribers: pharmacist prescribers.
Registered nurse prescribers in community health.
Registered nurse prescribers in diabetes health.
Registered nurse prescribers in primary health and speciality teams.
Designated prescribers complete additional post-graduate training to prescribe.

recall.q: What can and cannot a Registered Nurse do in relation to medications?
a: Key role: administer and monitor medications, assess patients, maintain documentation, ensure safe medication practices, and educate patients, caregivers and whānau.
CANNOT prescribe, unless holding the extra qualification as a designated nurse prescriber.
CANNOT modify prescriptions.
CAN administer under standing orders.
MAY administer drugs with a prescriber's verbal order, e.g. an order over the phone or given in an emergency.
Nurses are personally responsible — legally, morally and ethically — for every medication they administer, no matter who prescribed it.

recall.q: List the 8 Rights and the 2 Checks of safe medication administration as taught in this course.
a: 1. Right patient.  2. Right medication.  3. Right dose.  4. Right time.  5. Right route.
6. Right to refuse.
7. Right indication.
8. Right documentation.
+ Check expiry.
+ Check allergies.

recall.q: How is patient identity checked before giving a medication, in hospital and in aged care?
a: Nurses must check the patient's identity before giving medication, using three identifiers.
The NHI is part of the identification process in Aotearoa.
Inpatient setting: check the patient identification band, and ask the patient to state full name and date of birth.
Aged care / residential setting: residents may not wear ID bands, so use reliable alternatives, e.g. photographic verification.

recall.q: When are the three medication checks performed, and what is the rule about who administers?
a: Check the label of the medication against the medication chart or prescription.
Check 1 — before preparing.
Check 2 — after preparing.
Check 3 — before replacing the container.
Only administer medications that YOU prepare.

The Medicines Care Guides version: check the unit dose pack or label when getting it from storage; check the contents against the resident's medicine order; re-check the order and medicine prior to administering.

recall.q: What must a nurse do about the right dose? Give five points including the rules on cutting and crushing.
a: Know the usual dose range for medications being administered; if unsure, check, e.g. the NZ Formulary.
Use medication calculations.
Prepare medications accurately, e.g. syringes, graduated cups.
Cut tablets in half with a tablet cutter — and only if the tablet has a score mark.
Check with a pharmacist before crushing tablets.
Discuss with the prescriber if a more appropriate formulation, e.g. a liquid, is needed.

recall.q: Explain the "right time", including the tolerance for regular medications and what governs prn timing.
a: Medication must be given at the prescribed time AND frequency.
Timing may depend on whether it should be taken with food or on an empty stomach, on therapeutic drug monitoring, and on when the last dose was given.
Some medications are time-critical, e.g. insulin before meals.
Regular medications should be given within 30 minutes of the scheduled time.
prn medications require clinical judgement, e.g. a pain assessment before analgesia.
Always use 24-hour time.

recall.q: What must the nurse do if no route is documented on the prescription?
a: The prescriber's order must include a route, and the route must be appropriate for the medication, the patient and the intended therapeutic action.
If no route is documented the nurse must WITHHOLD the medication.
And contact the prescriber for clarification.
If the patient is unable to take the drug by the prescribed route, discuss with the prescriber.

recall.q: Describe the nurse's actions when a patient exercises the right to refuse.
a: Patients have the right to refuse a medication unless they are being treated under the Mental Health Act.
Explain the consequences to the patient, e.g. an increase in symptoms, or an infection not being treated.
Document the patient's reason for refusal.
Inform those necessary, e.g. the next shift RN, the prescriber and maybe whānau.
Discard refused medications — do not store them.

recall.q: What does "right indication" require of the administering nurse?
a: The nurse administering is accountable and requires knowledge about the indication for the medication.
Is it being given for the right reason?
This is especially important for prn medications, which require nurse-led assessment and clinical decision making.

recall.q: State the rules for right documentation, including prn and errors.
a: Record medication immediately after administration: date, time, dose, who administered.
NEVER document before you have actually administered it to the person.
When a dose is not given — e.g. refused, or the patient is unavailable because they are in a procedure — document this and the reason why.
Documentation for prn medications must include the nursing assessment before administering, and the nursing evaluation after.
Discuss and document any errors.

recall.q: Explain the expiry date check, including the two situations where an expiry date cannot be relied on.
a: An expiry date is a marker of the length of time that a medication is effective and safe.
It may be labelled expiry / expiry date / expires / exp, or use by / use before.
If only a month is supplied, e.g. July 2030, the expiry date is the end of that month.
You cannot rely on an expiry date if the medication has been REPACKAGED.
Or if it has NOT been stored as recommended by the manufacturer, e.g. kept dry, or kept in the fridge.
Medications repackaged by a pharmacist may only have a dispensing date — these should be kept no longer than 12 months after that date.

recall.q: Describe the allergy check, including the two acronyms.
a: Allergies are also called hypersensitivities.
Allergies — or confirmation of no allergies — should be documented in the medication chart.
AND the administering nurse should ask the patient about allergies.
NKA = no known allergies. NKDA = no known drug allergies.
An allergy to any medication would be a contraindication for its use.

recall.q: Where does medication administration fit into the Nursing Process? Give the assessment and evaluation points.
a: ASSESSMENT — take a health history: history relevant to pharmacokinetics (e.g. pregnancy, liver disease); what medications or substances they are taking; any allergies.
Also: any challenges with their medications, e.g. memory, or opening containers; cultural needs and preferences; are the indications for the medication there?
DIAGNOSIS — make decisions about the importance of the information gathered, and the implications for the patient.

PLANNING & IMPLEMENTING — use the 8 Rights when preparing and administering; use prn and standing order medications appropriately; advocate (e.g. for a medication review or an easier formulation to swallow); educate about medications.
EVALUATION — assess and document the therapeutic response; any non-therapeutic responses or adverse effects; the patient's knowledge of the medication; and their ability to self-manage it.

recall.q: What must the National Medication Chart contain under patient identification and prescriber requirements?
a: PATIENT IDENTIFICATION: full name; NHI number; date of birth; allergies and adverse reactions.
When relevant: body measurements (weight, height, body surface area) and gestational age at birth, e.g. for neonates.
PRESCRIBER REQUIREMENTS: date the order was written; medication name; dose and units.
Route of administration; frequency and/or specific administration times.
The prescriber's signature, linked to the sample signatures.

recall.q: Name the five special sections of the National Medication Chart, and the RN's own charting requirements.
a: Once-only medicines.
Verbal orders.
PRN medicines.
Fluid and infusion orders.
Oxygen and medical gases orders.
RN requirements: a signature/initials for each dose given, and non-administration codes when a dose is withheld or not given.
Student nurses also need the "check" initial.

mcq.q: How many Rights plus checks of safe medication administration does this course teach?
mcq.why: The deck teaches 8 Rights (patient, medication, dose, time, route, right to refuse, indication, documentation) plus 2 Checks (expiry, allergies), and explicitly notes the textbooks' five "do not cover all Rights you need to practice safely". The essay brief uses the same wording.

mcq.q: A regular medication is scheduled for 0800. Within what window should it be given?
mcq.why: "Regular medications should be given within 30 mins of scheduled time." prn medications instead require clinical judgement, e.g. a pain assessment.

mcq.q: A prescription states the medication, dose and frequency, but no route. The nurse should:
options: Give it by the most usual route for that drug
Ask another nurse which route to use
Withhold the medication and contact the prescriber
Give it orally and document the change
mcq.why: If no route is documented the nurse must withhold the medication and contact the prescriber for clarification. A nurse cannot modify a prescription.

mcq.q: A medication is repackaged by a pharmacist and shows only a dispensing date. It should be kept no longer than:
mcq.why: Repackaged medications may only carry a dispensing date, not an expiry date; the deck states these should be kept no longer than 12 months after the dispensing date.

mcq.q: A patient competently refuses a prescribed medication. Which action is NOT correct?
options: Explain the consequences of not taking it
Return the medication to the container for later use
Inform the next shift RN and the prescriber
mcq.why: Refused medications must be DISCARDED, not stored. The other three actions are all required.

mcq.q: When must a medication be documented as given?
options: Before administering, so it is not forgotten
At the end of the medication round
At the end of the shift
mcq.why: Record immediately after administration — date, time, dose, who administered. "Never document before you have actually administered it to the person."

mcq.q: Which professional group can prescribe ONLY with an additional qualification, and otherwise operates under standing orders?
mcq.why: Pharmacists cannot prescribe unless they hold the extra qualification as a Pharmacist Prescriber; they otherwise operate under standing orders. Midwives, optometrists and dentists are all authorised prescribers.

mcq.q: A tablet may be cut in half:
options: Any time a half dose is prescribed
Only with a tablet cutter, and only if it has a score mark
mcq.why: The deck: "Cut tablets in half with a tablet cutter (only if has a score mark)." Separately, check with a pharmacist before crushing any tablet.

mcq.q: "NKDA" documented in the medication chart means:
mcq.why: NKDA = no known drug allergies; NKA = no known allergies. Both are from the Must Know Abbreviations table, and both must still be confirmed by asking the patient.
mcq.src: Med Admin (1) 2026 slide 43 · Must Know Abbreviations 01.26

topics.name: Errors, Education & Health Literacy
topics.chapters: Module 5 · Med Admin (2) · HQSC three steps

recall.q: Define a medication error and explain how it differs from an adverse effect. Give four examples.
a: A medication error is "any preventable event that may cause or lead to inappropriate medication use or patient harm while the medication is in control of the healthcare professional, patient or consumer".
Different from an adverse effect of a drug — a medication error is often harm arising from human action.
Examples: a drug given to a patient with a known allergy; a wrong dosage dispensed from pharmacy.
Errors in the medication calculation; incorrectly deciphering handwriting.
Documentation errors leading to a dose being duplicated.
Most medication errors can be linked to an inconsistency in adhering to the 8 Rights + 2 Checks.

recall.q: Name six ways to prevent medication errors, with the reason for each.
a: Check labels carefully — medications may have similar names or containers, or similar colours and shapes.
Think: does the dose sound right? Most appropriate doses are one or two tablets, or one single-dose vial.
Check the decimal point — is it 0.1, 1.0 or 10?
Question sudden changes in dose — most dosages are increased gradually so the prescriber can monitor effects.
Learn about new medications before you administer them — unfamiliarity carries a higher risk of error; check the NZ Formulary.
Do not try to decipher illegible writing — when in doubt, ask the prescriber to clarify what they wrote.

recall.q: Describe the five steps for managing and reporting a medication error.
a: Acknowledge the error immediately.
Report promptly to the appropriate person, e.g. the charge nurse.
Document the error accurately and objectively in the patient notes.
Implement measures to counteract or minimise harm if required, e.g. monitoring.
Complete an incident report.

recall.q: What are the consequences of intentional concealment of a medication error?
a: [[Intentional concealment]] is not telling someone when you know you made an error.
The patient may be more at risk of injury, illness or death.
You will face disciplinary action.

recall.q: Explain nursing liability for medication errors.
a: Prescribers, pharmacists and nurses can all be held responsible when they make an error with medication — wrong dose prescribed, dispensed, or administered.
Nurses are liable for their actions AND omissions.
Nurses are liable for the duties they delegate to others.
Nurses are personally responsible — legally, morally and ethically — for every medication they administer, no matter who prescribed or dispensed it.

recall.q: Name the three steps to meeting health literacy needs, and state what Step 1 involves and why.
a: The ABCs: [[Ask]], [[Build]], [[Check]].
Step 1 — Ask questions to find out what people know.
Why: people bring prior knowledge, beliefs and feelings about medications; we connect new information to what they already know, to help them learn, understand and retain.
Why: we want to avoid repeating information people already know, which makes them disengage.
Think about WHO we ask — health information and skills may be held by an individual, or collectively by whānau and support people.
How: use a conversational friendly tone; ask open-ended questions ("What have you heard about this medicine?", "Please tell me…"); ask for demonstration; use pictorial resources.

recall.q: What does Step 2, Build, involve?
a: Connect new information to what people already know, feel and understand.
Use the words and phrases the person used in Step 1.
Pause after giving new information to let people think.
Explain the next steps: expected effects, possible adverse effects, and the follow-up plan.
Explain and repeat essential health terms — people need terms like "hypertension" and the generic medication name to talk about their condition.
Avoid medical jargon where possible (say "sore tummy" rather than "gastrointestinal problem"); if you must use a medical term, explain it in plain language.
Use visual resources: simple step-by-step diagrams with colour; with written resources, explain how the information is organised and highlight, underline or circle key ideas.

recall.q: What does Step 3, Check, involve — and whose responsibility is clarity?
a: Check how clear YOUR communication was.
Do not rely on minimal cues like nodding "yes"; avoid closed questions like "Do you understand?".
Use [[Teach back]] — ask people to explain in their own words what they need to do.
Use prompts if a small piece of information is missing; take responsibility if you were unclear and offer to re-explain.
This is NOT a test of the patient's cognition or intelligence — the responsibility for clear communication lies with you.
If the person does not recall the new information, consider how you delivered it (language, too much information, are they stressed or unwell?) and go back to Step 2 to explain it a different way.

recall.q: Name the five principles of Te Tiriti o Waitangi as taught in this course, with their English meanings.
recall.src: Med Admin (2) 2026 slide 33 (Nursing Council of NZ, 2025)
a: [[Tino Rangatiratanga]] — Self-determination.
[[Mana Taurite]] — Equity.
[[Whakamarumarutia]] — Active protection.
[[Kōwhiringa]] — Options.
[[Pātuitanga]] — Partnership.
Note: the "three Ps" (partnership, participation, protection) were developed in 1986 and are OUTDATED.

recall.q: Give one practical medication-education example for each of the five Te Tiriti principles.
a: Tino Rangatiratanga — ask "How do you feel about starting this medication?"; invite patient and whānau to share preferences before giving instructions; offer time to decide rather than rushing consent.

Mana Taurite — allow more time for education for health consumers who need it; adjust teaching to lived context (cost, transport, literacy, access to pharmacy); engage in advocacy. Equity is unequal distribution for equal outcome.

Whakamarumarutia — acknowledge and respect rongoā Māori or other cultural practices alongside prescribed medication, and advocate for the wider health team to do the same; be aware of body language, tone and power dynamics.
Kōwhiringa — offer alternatives where possible (timing, formulation, lifestyle); explain benefits and risks clearly; include whānau if the patient wishes; provide options for follow-up.
Pātuitanga — ask "Who would you like to be involved in this conversation?"; co-create a management plan aligning doses with daily routines; position the patient as a partner, not a passive recipient.

recall.q: What should a nurse teach a parent or caregiver about giving medicines to children?
a: Always store medicines out of reach and out of sight.
Always use a proper measuring cup, spoon or syringe.
Check with your pharmacist before crushing or cutting tablets.
Do not force a child to take medication — it can cause vomiting, choking or injury.
Instead try using an ice block to numb the taste buds first, or giving praise and a reward such as a sticker.

recall.q: How should medication education be adapted for toddlers and children?
a: Use age-appropriate language like "sore tummy".
Tell them the medicine will help them feel better.
Use similes or stories, e.g. for an antibiotic: "this medicine is like soldiers that are going to fight off the germs".
Do not lie — e.g. an immunisation is going to feel sore; focus on something nice to look forward to afterwards.
NEVER tell them that their medicine is lollies — risk of overdose.
Give simple choices, especially for younger children.

recall.q: How should medication education be adapted for teenagers?
a: Explain the mechanism of action in simple terms — why is this medication relevant to the young person (killing germs, replacing missing chemicals, stopping pain signals, slowing inflammation)?
Medicines have benefits and risks, so correct use (route and dose) is essential — e.g. taking extra paracetamol will not make a headache go away faster.
Teach them how to look out for adverse effects, and what to do.
Talk about whether alcohol or drugs affect their medications.
Emphasise that medicines should never be shared with others.
Encourage them to ask questions — they are developing independence.

recall.q: How should medication education be adapted for older adults?
a: Educate for self-management and adherence — explain purpose, dose, timing, route, expected benefits and common adverse effects.
Consider sensory needs and cognitive changes: allow extra time, minimise background noise, speak clearly and slowly, check hearing aids and glasses, use familiar names, provide large-print resources.
Plan around fatigue and energy levels.
Involve family/whānau and formal and informal carers — as long as the older adult gives consent.
Uphold dignity and autonomy.

mcq.q: A medication error is best defined as:
options: Any harmful effect caused by a medicine
Any preventable event that may cause or lead to inappropriate medication use or patient harm
Any dose given outside the therapeutic range
mcq.why: This is the NCC MERP definition the deck quotes. An adverse effect is harm caused by the medicine itself; a medication error is a preventable event, often from human action.

mcq.q: What is the FIRST step after realising you have made a medication error?
options: Document it in the patient notes
mcq.why: The sequence is: acknowledge immediately → report promptly to the appropriate person → document accurately and objectively → implement measures to minimise harm → complete an incident report.

mcq.q: Which question best fits Step 3 (Check) of the health literacy model?
options: "Can you tell me what you have to do, so I can check I explained it properly?"
"You'll be fine with this, won't you?"
mcq.why: That is teach-back, and it is phrased so responsibility sits with the nurse. The deck explicitly says to avoid closed questions like "Do you understand?" and not to rely on nodding.

mcq.q: Which set of Te Tiriti principles does the Nursing Council use, per this course?
options: Tino Rangatiratanga, Mana Taurite, Whakamarumarutia, Kōwhiringa, Pātuitanga
mcq.why: The deck lists the five NCNZ (2025) principles and notes in its own speaker notes that the "three Ps" of 1986 are OUTDATED.

mcq.q: Mana Taurite is best described as:
mcq.why: Mana Taurite = Equity — removing barriers and adapting communication so understanding is equitable. Equity is unequal distribution for equal outcome.

mcq.q: Which is NOT advice the deck gives about giving medicines to children?
options: Store medicines out of reach and out of sight
Use a proper measuring cup, spoon or syringe
Tell the child the medicine is lollies so they take it
Check with your pharmacist before crushing or cutting tablets
mcq.why: Never tell a child their medicine is lollies — the deck flags it as an overdose risk, and Case Study 1 turns on exactly this point.

mcq.q: A patient taking the combined oral contraceptive pill reports also taking St John's Wort. The documented risk is:
mcq.why: The deck's Case Study 2 speaker note, citing the NZ Formulary interactions checker: "Risks include breakthrough bleeding and contraception failure" — St John's Wort is an enzyme inducer.

topics.name: The Older Adult & Polypharmacy
topics.chapters: Module 6 · Knights ch. 41 · Potter & Perry ch. 30

recall.q: How is an older person defined in Aotearoa NZ, and what are the sub-categories?
a: An older person in Aotearoa NZ is defined as those aged 65 years and over.
"Young-old": 65–79 years.
"Old-old": 80+ years.
Frail elderly: a person 65 years or older with at least one debilitating condition.
There are wide variations in the rate of ageing between persons and within individuals — and age-related changes are not to be confused with disease-related changes.

recall.q: Give the figures for medication use in older adults, and the three reasons it is disproportionately high.
a: People over 65 years constitute about 12% of the population.
But consume 31% of prescribed medications.
Reason 1: increased severity of chronic illness.
Reason 2: presence of multiple pathologies (illnesses).
Reason 3: excessive prescribing.
Older adults take on average 4–5 prescribed medications, PLUS 2 over-the-counter medications.

recall.q: Describe the age-related changes to drug ABSORPTION, and state their clinical significance.
a: Slowed gastric emptying → delayed movement of medicines into the intestines.
Reduced GI motility and slower transit time → slower absorption.
Decreased intestinal surface area → reduced absorption efficiency.
These changes can delay overall drug absorption, but are often NOT clinically significant.

recall.q: Describe the three age-related changes to drug DISTRIBUTION and the effect of each.
a: Increased body fat → fat-soluble medications have a LONGER effect (stored in fat and released slowly).
Reduced total body water → water-soluble medications reach a HIGHER concentration, so have a SHORTER and STRONGER effect.
Lower protein binding → more free (active) drug circulating in the body, producing more effect.
Together these alter how drugs are distributed, affecting duration of action and potential toxicity.

recall.q: Describe the age-related changes to drug METABOLISM.
a: Slowed liver metabolism and reduced blood flow → affects how drugs are processed, e.g. reduced clearance of drugs with a high extraction ratio via the liver.
Some enzyme reactions are slowed (e.g. oxidation) while some are unaffected (e.g. conjugation).
Common age-related conditions like congestive heart failure further impair liver function, increasing the risk of drug accumulation and toxicity.

recall.q: Describe the age-related changes to renal EXCRETION and their consequence.
a: Reduced kidney function — nephron loss, reduced blood flow, lower glomerular filtration rate → slower elimination of renally cleared drugs.
Slower renal clearance raises plasma drug levels and extends the half-lives of drugs and active metabolites → increased risk of toxicity.
Heart failure may further reduce renal perfusion, increasing the risk of drug accumulation.
If renal impairment is suspected, prescribers should request renal function tests and use therapeutic drug monitoring to adjust doses safely.

recall.q: Explain the pharmacodynamic changes of ageing.
a: Ageing can cause either INCREASED or DECREASED drug effects, depending on the drug and receptor involved.
Changes occur because of fewer receptors at the target site,
and/or altered receptor responsiveness — increased or decreased — due to changes in second-messenger signalling.
Down-regulation of receptors may also occur due to prolonged exposure to drugs.

recall.q: Name the six most common adverse effects of medications in older adults.
a: Falls.
[[Orthostatic hypotension]].
Delirium.
Renal failure.
Gastrointestinal bleeding.
Intracranial bleeding.

recall.q: Give the four reasons adverse drug reactions increase in frequency in older adults.
a: Age-related pharmacokinetic changes — altered distribution of drugs and reduced clearance from the bloodstream.
Age-related pharmacodynamic changes — increased receptor sensitivity to some drugs, especially CNS and cardiovascular medications.
Higher burden of illness and polypharmacy — a greater number of illnesses means more medications and more interactions.
Inappropriate prescribing and poor monitoring — e.g. use of drugs with a narrow therapeutic index.

recall.q: What is the Beers Criteria, and give the two examples from the lecture with their adverse effects.
a: [[Beers Criteria]] is a tool widely used to guide prescribers on the drugs that should be avoided or used with caution in older adults.
