NSAIDs (e.g. ibuprofen) — avoid chronic use. Adverse effects: gastritis, gastrointestinal bleeding, ulceration.
Digoxin — avoid as first-line therapy for atrial fibrillation. Adverse effects: nausea, vomiting, cardiac dysrhythmias, visual disorders, mental status changes, hallucinations.

recall.q: Under what two conditions may a medication be crushed, and what three outcomes can crushing cause?
a: Crushing may make the medication less effective, ineffective, or dangerous — e.g. if enteric-coated but then rapidly absorbed, it may cause harm.
Medications should only be crushed if a pharmacist advises that this does not compromise the medication,
AND this is in the best interest of the patient.

recall.q: Define polypharmacy and list the five risks it raises.
a: [[Polypharmacy]] is the concurrent use of multiple medications, usually 5 or more.
The word has the connotation that too many, or unnecessary, drugs have been prescribed or are being taken.
Increased risk of adverse effects.
Increased risk of drug–drug interactions.
Medication non-adherence.
Falls.
Mortality.

recall.q: Give the Auckland retirement-village prevalence figures for polypharmacy.
a: A study of 578 retirement village residents from 33 different retirement villages in Auckland, median age 81.6 years.
51.8% met criteria for polypharmacy (≥5 medicines).
5.7% met criteria for [[Hyperpolypharmacy]] (≥10 medicines).
Residents took a mean of 4.8 regular medicines plus 0.7 as-required medicines.

recall.q: Give six reasons polypharmacy occurs.
a: More co-morbidities in older adults.
Multiple prescribers — e.g. a GP and an outpatient clinic.
Medications can be advertised in Aotearoa NZ.
Medications are easier to access than lifestyle changes such as exercise.
Medications not being reviewed regularly by a prescriber — can anything be de-prescribed? GP consults are 15 minutes.
Use of duplicate medications (brand names).
Concurrent use of traditional therapies.
The [[Prescribing cascade]].

recall.q: Name five strategies to manage polypharmacy.
a: Systematic medication review.
Use of validated prescribing tools, e.g. [[Beers Criteria]].
[[Deprescribing]].
Patient-centred decision-making.
Good quality documentation.
Nurses may be involved as part of the multi-disciplinary team and/or as an advocate for polypharmacy review.

recall.q: Besides older adults, which groups are at risk of polypharmacy?
a: Elderly adults are the highest-risk group, but polypharmacy is not only an older person's health issue.
Infants and children with complex conditions.
People with disabilities.
People with cognitive impairment.
People with chronic mental health conditions.
Individuals in institutional settings, e.g. prison or a residential facility.
People with language or communication barriers, who are more susceptible to prescribing errors and miscommunication.

recall.q: Give four pieces of key legislation and guidance covering medication use in aged care.
a: Old People's Home Regulations (1987).
Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act (2003).
Code of Health and Disability Services Consumers' Rights.
Medicines Care Guides for Residential Aged Care (2011).
NCNZ Standards of Practice (2025) and Code of Conduct (2012).

recall.q: Distinguish errors of commission from errors of omission in older people, with two examples of each.
a: [[Error of commission]] is an error of DOING: taking the wrong dose; taking the wrong medication due to look-alike packaging.
Also: taking medicine incorrectly with food, beverages or other substances; taking medication from someone else or a pet; taking expired medication; storing medication incorrectly.
[[Error of omission]] is an error of NOT DOING: forgetting to take medication; taking too low a dose (sub-therapeutic).
Also: forgetting instructions from the doctor or pharmacist; taking a dose at the wrong time.

mcq.q: People over 65 are about 12% of the NZ population. What share of prescribed medications do they consume?
mcq.why: The deck: people over 65 constitute about 12% of the population but consume 31% of prescribed medications.

mcq.q: In an older adult, reduced total body water means a water-soluble drug will have a:
mcq.why: Less body water means the same dose sits at a higher concentration — "like a stronger cordial" in the deck's own note — giving a shorter, stronger effect. Increased body FAT is what gives fat-soluble drugs a longer effect.

mcq.q: Which age-related pharmacokinetic change is described in the lecture as "often not clinically significant"?
mcq.why: Slowed gastric emptying, reduced motility and decreased intestinal surface area delay absorption, "but often not clinically significant". Reduced excretion and metabolism are what actually drive accumulation and toxicity.

mcq.q: Polypharmacy is usually defined as the concurrent use of:
mcq.why: Polypharmacy is the concurrent use of multiple medications, usually 5 or more. Ten or more is hyperpolypharmacy.

mcq.q: Under the Beers Criteria, chronic use of NSAIDs such as ibuprofen in older adults should be:
mcq.why: The Beers table in the deck: NSAIDs — "avoid chronic use", because of gastritis, gastrointestinal bleeding and ulceration.

mcq.q: Which is an error of OMISSION rather than commission?
mcq.why: Errors of omission are errors of not doing — forgetting to take medication, taking too low a dose, forgetting instructions, or taking a dose at the wrong time. The other three are errors of commission.

mcq.q: A medication may be crushed:
options: Whenever the patient has difficulty swallowing
Only if a pharmacist advises it does not compromise the medication AND it is in the patient's best interest
Only if it is enteric coated
mcq.why: Both conditions must hold. Crushing can make a medication less effective, ineffective or dangerous — an enteric-coated tablet that is crushed becomes rapidly absorbed.

mcq.q: The term that has replaced "compliance" in describing whether a patient takes their medication as intended is:
mcq.why: The deck notes directly that adherence has replaced the older term "compliance".

recall.q: Why does this session focus on pharmacokinetics rather than pharmacodynamics?
a: There are both PK and PD changes in pregnancy, breastfeeding, neonates, infants and children.
Pharmacokinetic changes (what the body does to the drug) in these groups are easier to predict.
Pharmacodynamic changes (what the drug does to the body) in pregnancy and children are much more complex, highly variable, and are poorly defined in textbooks.

recall.q: How do medications reach and affect the foetus, and when is the most vulnerable time?
a: Any substance the pregnant person's body absorbs can reach the foetus via maternal circulation.
Medication use should be limited; prescribers consider whether the benefit to the pregnant person outweighs any risk to the foetus.

Even when trying to get pregnant, persons with a uterus should talk to a health professional before taking any medications — including complementary/alternative medicines and chemicals — because effects may occur before pregnancy is recognised.
The most vulnerable time is the first few weeks of development.

recall.q: Describe the pharmacokinetic changes of pregnancy under all four ADME headings.
a: ABSORPTION: delayed gastric emptying and reduced gut motility (may increase OR decrease absorption); vomiting can prevent full absorption.
DISTRIBUTION: increased maternal plasma volume dilutes drug concentration; increased body fat stores lipophilic drugs, lowering plasma levels; drugs can diffuse across the placenta to the foetus.
METABOLISM (maternal): hepatic enzyme activity can change — caffeine metabolism is slower, paracetamol metabolism is faster.
METABOLISM (foetal): the foetus has immature enzymes, so slow metabolism and longer drug effects; metabolites may accumulate in amniotic fluid, extending exposure.
EXCRETION: increased renal blood flow increases elimination of renally cleared drugs, which may require higher or more frequent doses.

recall.q: Define a teratogen, state the highest-risk period, and name four sources.
a: A [[Teratogen]] is any substance or factor that can cause developmental abnormalities in a foetus during pregnancy.
Highest risk is during the first trimester (weeks 0–12).
Caused by prescription drugs, OTC medicines, herbal products, aromatherapy oils, alcohol, nicotine, and drugs of misuse/abuse.
Teratogens can cause physical birth defects, developmental delay, intellectual disability and other health problems.

recall.q: Give the four teratogen examples from the lecture table, with critical period and potential defect.
a: Alcohol — <12 weeks: fetal alcohol syndrome, heart defects, CNS abnormalities. >24 weeks: low birthweight, delay in development.
Cocaine — 2nd–3rd trimester: premature labour and delivery, intracranial bleeding.
Isotretinoin (an oral acne medication) — >15 days: hydrocephalus, CNS abnormalities, foetal death.
Tetracycline antibiotics — >20 weeks: stained teeth, bone growth defects.

recall.q: Describe the effects of alcohol, nicotine, cannabis, caffeine and opioid dependence on the foetus.
a: Most drugs of dependence are lipid-soluble, so they cross the placenta and affect foetal development.
Alcohol: depression of the foetal nervous system and developmental abnormalities — risk of Foetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder.
Nicotine (smoking/vaping): risk of pregnancy loss, preterm birth, low birthweight and jaundice.
Cannabis: does not appear to alter gene expression, but long-term risks are not yet known.
Caffeine: safe in small amounts — note reduced clearance in pregnancy.
Opioid dependence (e.g. heroin, methadone): newborns may experience withdrawal — irritability, tremors and seizures — and need treatment with opioids at birth to manage withdrawal symptoms.

recall.q: What is the medication pregnancy category system, and what do A and X mean?
a: The scale ranges from A (no harm) → B1, B2, B3 → C → D → X (high risk, contraindicated).

[[Pregnancy category A]]: drugs taken by a large number of pregnant or potentially pregnant people without any proven increase in the frequency of malformations or other harmful effects on the foetus — e.g. paracetamol.
[[Pregnancy category X]]: the most dangerous; should not be used if there is any possible or confirmed pregnancy.

recall.q: On what three factors does medication transfer to a breastfed infant depend, and what is the guiding principle?
a: Most medicines can enter breast milk and may affect the infant.
Maternal drug plasma concentration.
Amount of milk consumed.
Lipid solubility of the drug.
Guiding principle: maintaining maternal health is essential, so necessary medications should NOT automatically be stopped.

recall.q: Which drugs concentrate most in breastmilk, what effects can they have on the infant, and what advice applies to alcohol, caffeine, nicotine and methamphetamine?
a: Drugs that affect the nervous system and are lipid-soluble (e.g. morphine or codeine) concentrate more in breastmilk.
Effects on the infant may include sedation, and a reduced suckling reflex with poor feeding.
Alcohol: plan feeds to minimise exposure.
Caffeine: safe in moderate amounts.
Nicotine: can increase the risk of [[SUDI]]; nicotine-replacement therapy and working towards smoking cessation are encouraged.
If using some illicit drugs, e.g. methamphetamine, breastfeeding is not recommended.

recall.q: What three risks does a prescriber balance when a breastfeeding parent needs medication?
a: Benefits of continued breastfeeding for the breastfeeding parent and the infant.
Risks of infant medication exposure.
Risks to the breastfeeding parent if essential medications are stopped.
Most medications can be used with caution, but evaluate individually — and seek advice from the prescriber and/or pharmacist.

recall.q: "Children are just miniature adults." True or false — and give four reasons.
a: FALSE. Children are physiologically different to adults and are changing/developing constantly.
Lack of protective mechanisms and barriers.
Poor temperature regulation.
Poor homeostatic mechanisms.
Different body composition — e.g. higher body water (75%), lower fat, lower bone mass.

recall.q: Give the age definitions for preterm, full term, neonate, infant, child and adolescent.
a: [[Preterm]]: birth at less than 36 weeks gestation.
[[Full term]]: birth at 36 to 40+ weeks gestation.
[[Neonate]]/newborn: less than 4 weeks old.
[[Infant]]: 5 weeks to 1 year.
[[Child]]: 1 to 12 years.
[[Adolescent]]: 12 to 16 years.

recall.q: Describe the pharmacokinetics of the neonate.
a: Physiological immaturity — e.g. thin skin and low stomach acid — can INCREASE drug absorption.
Poor thermoregulation and a higher risk of dehydration.
Immature drug-metabolising enzymes, e.g. reduced metabolism of paracetamol.
Immature kidneys → slower drug clearance → prolonged half-life.
Immature blood–brain barrier → higher CNS toxicity risk.

recall.q: Describe the pharmacokinetics of infants and children, including how it changes with age.
a: Before age 12 months, renal excretion is slower, giving a longer half-life of drugs.
By 1 year, absorption, distribution and excretion are similar to adults.
Hepatic metabolism is FASTER until about 10 years, so higher mg/kg doses may be required.
Infants have a higher percentage of body water → increased distribution and lower concentration of water-soluble drugs → may need higher doses.
Paediatric doses are usually weight-based (mg/kg).
Formulation challenges: taste masking, and inability to swallow tablets.

recall.q: Why should paracetamol elixir not be given under 3 months or 5 kg without medical advice?
a: Narrow therapeutic range → higher risk of overdose.
Delayed development of drug-metabolising hepatic enzymes → decreased rate of metabolism.
Which increases blood levels of toxic metabolites → risk of liver injury.
From age 3 months, paracetamol may be given using an mg/kg dose.

recall.q: Tama is 3 years old and weighs 17.7 kg. Using a single dose of 15 mg/kg, what is his paracetamol dose in mg — and why is an adult dose unsafe?
a: Single dose = 15 mg/kg.
From Paracetamol 250 mg/5 mL that is 5.3 mL (the Healthify calculator answer).
A normal adult dose is 1 g / 1000 mg — nearly four times Tama's dose, and not safe for him.

recall.q: List seven considerations when administering medications to children.
a: Appropriate dose prescribed.
Developmentally appropriate formulation and route, e.g. an oral elixir.
Informed consent from the legal guardian — plus assent from the child.
Communication and appropriate terminology.
Tools: simple choices, distraction and play.
Honesty.
Secure assistance when needed, e.g. a parent.

mcq.q: The highest-risk period for teratogenic effects is:
mcq.why: The deck: "Highest risk is during first trimester (week 0 – 12)." Cocaine is the one example in the table whose critical period is the 2nd–3rd trimester.

mcq.q: Which is a Pregnancy Category A medication in the lecture's example?
mcq.why: Category A drugs have been taken by a large number of pregnant people without any proven increase in malformations or other harmful effects — paracetamol is the deck's example. Category X is the contraindicated end of the scale.

mcq.q: Renal excretion in pregnancy:
options: Decreases, so lower doses are needed
Increases, so higher or more frequent doses may be required
Stops entirely for renally cleared drugs
mcq.why: Increased renal blood flow increases elimination of renally cleared drugs, which may require higher or more frequent doses.

mcq.q: A neonate has an immature blood–brain barrier. The main consequence is:
mcq.why: The deck lists immature BBB → higher CNS toxicity risk, alongside immature enzymes (reduced metabolism) and immature kidneys (slower clearance, prolonged half-life).

mcq.q: Hepatic metabolism in children is:
options: Slower than adults until about 10 years
Faster than adults until about 10 years, so higher mg/kg doses may be needed
The same as adults from birth
mcq.why: Hepatic metabolism is faster until about 10 years, which may require higher mg/kg doses. It is the NEONATE whose enzymes are immature and metabolism reduced.

mcq.q: Which drugs concentrate most in breastmilk?
options: Water-soluble drugs that do not affect the nervous system
Lipid-soluble drugs that affect the nervous system, e.g. morphine or codeine
Drugs that are highly protein bound
mcq.why: The deck: drugs that affect the nervous system and are lipid-soluble concentrate more in breastmilk, and can cause infant sedation and a reduced suckling reflex with poor feeding.

mcq.q: Tetracycline antibiotics taken after 20 weeks of pregnancy are associated with:
options: Stained teeth and bone growth defects
mcq.why: From the teratogen table: tetracycline antibiotics, >20 weeks, stained teeth and bone growth defects. Hydrocephalus/CNS is isotretinoin; premature labour/intracranial bleeding is cocaine.

mcq.q: A neonate is defined as:
mcq.why: Neonate/newborn = less than 4 weeks old. 5 weeks to 1 year is an infant; before 36 weeks gestation is preterm; 1–12 years is a child.

recall.q: Define Act, Regulation, Amendment, Policy and Guideline.
a: [[Act (statute)]]: laws made by parliament (government).
[[Regulation]]: made underneath Acts, providing instructions about how the Acts are enforced.
[[Amendment]]: changes (updates) made to an Act or Regulation.
Policies & procedures: enforceable rules or instructions within an organisation, e.g. a Medications Policy.
[[Guideline]]: best practice advice on how to do things.

recall.q: Name the three key Acts governing medications in Aotearoa NZ, with their accompanying regulations.
a: The Medicines Act 1981, and the Medicines Regulations 1984.
The Misuse of Drugs Act 1975, and the Misuse of Drugs Regulations 1977.
The Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act 2003.

recall.q: What does the Medicines Act 1981 cover and do? Give five points.
a: Covers all "medicines".
"Medicines" includes all products used for therapeutic purposes, including cosmetics and dietary supplements with therapeutic claims.
Classifies medicines — prescription, restricted, pharmacy-only, general sale.
Sets rules for clinical trials, manufacturing, advertising and sale.
Defines who can prescribe.

recall.q: What does the Misuse of Drugs Act 1975 do? Give four points, plus the two storage rules.
a: Defines drug classes — controlled versus uncontrolled.
Regulates prescribing of controlled drugs.
Defines penalties and gives police enforcement powers.
Controls precursor substances.
Medication rooms must be locked when not in use.
Controlled drugs must be kept double-locked.

recall.q: Describe the three classes of controlled drug with examples.
a: [[Class A controlled drug]]: high potential for abuse; very high risk of harm; not prescribed for medical use. E.g. heroin, LSD, cocaine, methamphetamine.

[[Class B controlled drug]]: includes drugs of dependence; high risk of harm; restrictions on prescribing and dispensing; must be kept in a double-locked safe. E.g. morphine, methylphenidate (Ritalin).
[[Class C controlled drug]]: lower potential for abuse but may lead to dependence; moderate risk of harm; can be prescribed "normally". E.g. codeine, diazepam.

recall.q: Define possession and supply under the Misuse of Drugs Act.
a: Illegal drugs are unlawful to use, possess or supply unless you have legal authority.
[[Possession]]: having a drug in your control, e.g. in your pocket, bag, car or bedroom. Only certain people may lawfully possess controlled drugs, e.g. health professionals and emergency services.
[[Supply]]: making a drug available to someone else, including giving or selling.

recall.q: Name the four regulators of NZ medications and their functions.
a: Medsafe — regulates medicines and devices for safety and quality.
PHARMAC — funding and subsidy decisions.
Health Research Council (HRC) — clinical trial approval and oversight.
Centre for Adverse Reactions Monitoring (CARM) — monitoring and investigation of adverse reactions.

recall.q: What is the purpose of the HPCAA 2003, and what four things does it require of Registered Nurses?
a: Purpose: protects public safety, by ensuring practitioners maintain ongoing competence and fitness to practise and work within defined scopes of practice, and by limiting restricted activities to qualified, registered practitioners.
Requires a scope of practice, defined by the regulatory authority (the Nursing Council of New Zealand).
Requires [[Annual Practising Certificate (APC)]]s, renewed annually to legally practise, and searchable on the public register.
Requires clinical and cultural competence, demonstrated through Nursing Council processes (portfolios), with Te Tiriti o Waitangi obligations.

Provides legal accountability through disciplinary pathways — preventing practice outside of scope, preventing unqualified people claiming to be an RN, and allowing RNs to be reviewed, restricted or suspended.

recall.q: Name the six pou of the NCNZ Standards of Competence for Registered Nurses.
a: Māori Health.
Cultural Safety.
Whanaungatanga and Communication.
Pūkengatanga and Evidence-Informed Nursing Practice.
Manaakitanga and People-Centred Care.
Rangatiratanga and Leadership.

recall.q: Define cultural safety as the Nursing Council does, and state what "culture" includes.
a: [[Cultural safety]] is "the effective nursing practice of a person or family from another culture, and is determined BY THAT PERSON OR FAMILY".
Culture includes, but is not restricted to: age or generation; gender; sexual orientation; occupation and socioeconomic status.
Ethnic origin or migrant experience; religious or spiritual belief; and disability.
The nurse will have undertaken a process of reflection on their own cultural identity, and will recognise the impact their personal culture has on their professional practice.

recall.q: How does the RN scope of practice relate to medication? Give six points.
a: RNs follow laws and policies to safely administer medications.
Use clinical judgement to assess medication needs and responses.
Communicate effectively with prescribers, pharmacists, patients and whānau.
Uphold Te Tiriti and cultural safety in medication-related activities.
Delegate medication tasks appropriately.
Remain professionally accountable for every medication they give or supervise.

recall.q: List the eight principles of the NCNZ Code of Conduct.
a: 1. Respect the dignity and individuality of health consumers.
2. Respect the cultural needs and values of health consumers.
3. Work in partnership with health consumers to promote and protect their well-being.
4. Maintain health consumer trust by providing safe and competent care.
5. Respect health consumers' privacy and confidentiality.
6. Work respectfully with colleagues to best meet health consumers' needs.
7. Act with integrity to justify health consumers' trust.
8. Maintain public trust and confidence in the nursing profession.

recall.q: Give a pharmacology example for Code of Conduct principles 2, 4 and 7.
a: Principle 2 (cultural needs and values): checking whether medication ingredients conflict with cultural beliefs, e.g. gelatin capsules.
Principle 4 (safe and competent care): double-checking with another nurse before administering a vaccination you have not given before.
Principle 7 (integrity): report medication errors honestly and immediately.

recall.q: Name the seven Māori values in the NZNO Code of Ethics 2019 and summarise each.
a: [[Rangatiratanga (NZNO)]] — Māori have the right to self-determination.
[[Manaakitanga (NZNO)]] — the way we make people feel welcome and ensure their mana is upheld through kindness, respect and care.
[[Tika]] — what is right and proper: truth, correctness, justice, fairness and human rights.
[[Whanaungatanga (NZNO)]] — establishing relationships and recognising whānau connections.
[[Wairuatanga]] — acknowledging that spiritual existence is essential and must be nourished.
[[Kotahitanga]] — unity, togetherness and collective action that encourages all people to contribute.
[[Kaitiakitanga]] — guardianship and stewardship, recognising responsibility to protect land, resources and future generations.

recall.q: Name the nine Western values in the NZNO Code of Ethics 2019 and summarise each.
a: [[Autonomy]] — the right of individuals or groups to self-determination and informed choices.
[[Beneficence]] — "doing good": taking actions that lead to outcomes regarded as worthwhile.
[[Non-maleficence]] — "causing no harm": the obligation to avoid, prevent and minimise harm.
[[Justice]] — the responsibility to treat people fairly and equitably.
[[Confidentiality]] — protecting the privacy of written, spoken or observed information.
[[Veracity]] — requires actions and communication to be truthful and honest.
[[Fidelity]] — the obligation to remain faithful to commitments, keep promises and maintain trust.
Guardianship of environment and resources — society's responsibility to respect, protect and sustain the environment and its resources.
Being professional — acting with accountability, integrity and competence.

recall.q: State the three exceptions to veracity, and the three grounds for breaking confidentiality.
a: VERACITY exceptions: therapeutic privilege — withholding information to prevent serious harm.
Patient preference — the patient asks not to know their prognosis.
Emergencies — the patient may be unconscious but need life-saving treatment.
CONFIDENTIALITY may be broken where there is risk of harm to self (self-inflicted).
Risk of harm to self (by another).
Risk of harm to another person.

recall.q: Summarise the four key documents by type, purpose, authority and enforceability.
a: HPCAA 2003 — legislation regulating health practitioners; provides the legal framework nurses must practise under; authority: New Zealand Parliament; ENFORCEABLE — law for all regulated health professionals.

NCNZ Standards of Competence — regulatory competency standards; define what nurses must be able to do (skills, knowledge, behaviours); authority: Nursing Council of New Zealand; ENFORCEABLE — required to keep an APC.
NCNZ Code of Conduct — regulatory behaviour standards; defines how nurses must behave professionally; authority: Nursing Council of New Zealand; ENFORCEABLE — NCNZ can discipline for breaches.

NZNO Code of Ethics — professional ethical practice guideline; defines how nurses should think and act ethically; authority: New Zealand Nurses Organisation; a GUIDELINE, but expected to be used by all RNs.

recall.q: Summarise the three legal cases against nurses in the lecture, with the issue and the outcome.
a: Nurse P (2005): removed two capsules of morphine sulphate (a Class B controlled drug) from a rest home cabinet for his own use, replacing the contents with powdered sucrose. Issues: theft, unlawful possession of a controlled drug. Outcome: convicted of theft, and de-registered.

Nurse H (2006): stole vials of morphine, pethidine and fentanyl from a locked drug safe, removed some contents for his own use and returned the vials to maintain inventory integrity; also took metronidazole and flucloxacillin.
Nurse H outcome: charges of theft of controlled drugs, procuring or possessing other opioids, and possession of prescription medicine without reasonable excuse. Registration cancelled.

Nurse D (2013): gave a patient the wrong medication, did not check it was appropriate nor check pulse or blood pressure, realised 20 minutes later, and took two days to report. The patient died two hours later; the medication "accelerated the patient's already expected demise".

Nurse D outcome: guilty of professional misconduct, suspended and fined $12,000; required to complete additional courses in medication administration, pharmacology and professional ethics, six months' supervision when administering medications, and no duty-coordinator or leadership role for six months. She left nursing voluntarily.

recall.q: What does medication legislation mean for the Registered Nurse? Give five points.
a: Nurses cannot prescribe.
Nurses may administer prescription or restricted medications only with a valid prescription.
Know the relevant legislation and your organisation's policies for storing, handling and administering medications.
Nurses have access to controlled and uncontrolled medicines — misuse of that access is unsafe and illegal.
Always admit mistakes and ask for help if unsure.

mcq.q: Morphine is which class of controlled drug under the Misuse of Drugs Act 1975?
mcq.why: Class B includes drugs of dependence, carries a high risk of harm, has restrictions on prescribing and dispensing, and must be kept in a double-locked safe — morphine and methylphenidate are the deck's examples.

mcq.q: Which Act requires Registered Nurses to hold an Annual Practising Certificate?
options: The Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act 2003
mcq.why: The HPCAA 2003 requires a scope of practice set by the Nursing Council, annual practising certificates, clinical and cultural competence, and provides legal accountability.

mcq.q: Cultural safety is determined by:
options: The person or family receiving the care
mcq.why: The NCNZ definition: "the effective nursing practice of a person or family from another culture, and is determined by that person or family."

mcq.q: Which is NOT one of the six pou of the NCNZ Standards of Competence?
mcq.why: The six pou are Māori Health; Cultural Safety; Whanaungatanga and Communication; Pūkengatanga and Evidence-Informed Nursing Practice; Manaakitanga and People-Centred Care; Rangatiratanga and Leadership. Kaitiakitanga is an NZNO Code of Ethics value, not a pou.

mcq.q: A nurse withholds a patient's prognosis because the patient has explicitly asked not to be told. This is an exception to:
mcq.why: Veracity is the duty to tell the truth; the three exceptions are therapeutic privilege, patient preference, and emergencies.

mcq.q: "Treating people fairly and equitably (not equally)" is the definition of which Western value?
mcq.why: Justice — be fair; treat people fairly and equitably, ensure fair access to care and unbiased decision-making. The deck explicitly contrasts equitably with equally.

mcq.q: Which document is a GUIDELINE rather than an enforceable standard?
mcq.why: From the summary table: the NZNO Code of Ethics "is a guideline, but expected to be used by all RNs". The other three are enforceable — by law, by APC requirement, and by NCNZ discipline respectively.

mcq.q: Checking whether gelatin capsules conflict with a patient's beliefs is an example of which Code of Conduct principle?
mcq.why: Principle 2 is to respect the cultural needs and values of health consumers, and gelatin capsules are the deck's own example.

mcq.q: In the 2013 case, what did the Nursing Council identify in addition to giving the wrong medication?
options: She was not wearing an ID badge
She took two days to report the error
She was working a double shift
mcq.why: Nurse D did not check the medication was appropriate nor check pulse or blood pressure, realised 20 minutes later, and took two days to report the error. She was found guilty of professional misconduct, suspended and fined $12,000.

recall.q: Give the cost, timescale and attrition figures for drug development.
a: The cost of developing a drug from active compound to marketable drug costs millions of dollars.
The development of a new drug can take 10–20 years.
According to USA statistics, only 5 in 5000 compounds progress to human testing.

recall.q: Name the five key phases of the drug development pathway.
a: Discovery & Development — early laboratory research to identify promising compounds.
[[Preclinical research]] — safety testing in laboratory models (sometimes animals) before human participation.
Clinical Trials — multi-phase studies involving people, to evaluate safety and effectiveness.
Medsafe Review — detailed review of data to approve or reject the drug.
Post-Market Monitoring — Medsafe continues safety surveillance after public release.

recall.q: Which three bodies must a developer apply to before a clinical trial can begin in NZ, and what does each assess?
a: Medsafe — review of preclinical studies, pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics, chemical stability and quality.
[[SCOTT]] (Standing Committee on Therapeutic Trials) — assesses the science, safety and appropriateness of the trial design.
[[HDEC]] (Health and Disability Ethics Committees) — checks for ethical compliance.
Developers must include: animal study data including adverse effects, data from any prior human research, and study plans.

recall.q: Describe the four phases of clinical research, with participant numbers, duration and progression rate.
a: [[Phase 1 trial]] — safety and dosage. 20–100 participants (healthy or with the condition). Several months. ~70% progress.
[[Phase 2 trial]] — efficacy and side effects. Several hundred participants with the condition. Months to 2 years. ~33% progress.
[[Phase 3 trial]] — confirming safety in large patient populations. 300–3000 participants with the condition. 1–4 years. 25–30% progress.
[[Phase 4 trial]] — long-term safety and effectiveness. Several thousand participants with the condition. Years.
The phases act like a funnel process.

recall.q: What five things do developers determine when designing a clinical trial?
a: Who qualifies — inclusion and exclusion criteria.
Sample size and study duration.
Methods to reduce bias, e.g. control groups.
Dosage and administration methods.
Data collection and analysis plans.

recall.q: Name the four key ethical issues in clinical trials, and the central ethical tension.
a: The key tension: the duty to care for current patients versus the duty to advance science for future patients.
Informed consent.
Use of placebos.
Use of randomisation.
Protection of vulnerable patients.
The history of human research includes serious abuses, e.g. unethical experiments on vulnerable groups.

recall.q: What must informed consent for a clinical trial be, and what four things must participants understand?
a: Consent must be voluntary, competent, and adequately informed.
Participants must understand the risks and potential benefits.
All study procedures.
That participation is voluntary.
That research is NOT the same as personalised treatment.
Consent can be withdrawn at ANY time.

recall.q: When is placebo use ethically acceptable, and when is it problematic?
a: Placebos are used with "control" participants to demonstrate the effect of a new drug.
Problematic if placebo recipients risk harm or worsening of their condition.
Acceptable when no proven treatment exists.
Or where necessary for methodology, without causing serious harm.

recall.q: What ethical issues does randomisation raise?
a: In randomised controlled trials, participants may be randomised to receive treatment or placebo, to increase the validity of the research.
Randomisation may deny participants the currently best-known treatment.
There needs to be genuine professional justification that one treatment is not known to be better than another.

recall.q: What issues arise in protecting vulnerable patients in trials?
a: Strict regulations in some countries can push trials to low-protection countries.
Over-protection can conflict with autonomy — a patient may want to choose higher personal risk.
Clinical trials may offer to reimburse participants.
Higher concern e.g. in cancer treatment trials, due to patients being in life-threatening situations.

recall.q: Name the five types of medication advertising seen in NZ, and describe each.
a: [[Direct-to-consumer advertising]] — promotes specific branded prescription medicines directly to the public, highlighting benefits, uses and risks.
[[Health-seeking advertising]] (disease awareness) — educates audiences about a health condition; may directly or indirectly encourage interest in a related brand.
[[Reminder ad]]s — mention the drug name only, without stating what it treats.
Professional/journal ads — aimed at healthcare professionals, focusing on clinical evidence, trial data and prescribing information.
Digital & social media marketing — uses online channels including influencers, targeted ads and social media content, often emphasising benefits more strongly than risks.

recall.q: What is unusual about medication advertising in Aotearoa NZ?
a: Aotearoa NZ is one of only two developed countries in the world that permits medication companies to advertise direct to the consumer.
(The deck's speaker note gives the other country as the USA.)

recall.q: What does the Therapeutic and Health Advertising Code require of medicine advertisements? Give six points.
a: Ads must be responsible, truthful, and not misleading.
Claims must be substantiated — have credible evidence.
Ads must not mislead or exaggerate the benefits.
Ads must include key safety information.
Any testimonials must reflect genuine experiences.
Endorsements from celebrities or health professionals cannot imply guaranteed outcomes.
Advertising unapproved medicines (not signed off by Medsafe) is prohibited, even to health professionals.

recall.q: How can a health professional accidentally breach advertising law, and what is exempt?
a: Advertising is defined broadly — it includes VERBAL advertising — so health professionals need to be careful about recommending or praising a product (brand) over another.
When giving information about a medication brand, health professionals must give information that is factual (evidence-based) and balanced, following the advertising rules.
EXEMPT: giving patients individualised advice about medications, using generic names, for their health condition.

mcq.q: Roughly how many of 5000 compounds progress to human testing?
mcq.why: "According to USA statistics only 5 in 5000 compounds progress to human testing." Development also costs millions and takes 10–20 years.

mcq.q: Which clinical trial phase focuses on SAFETY AND DOSAGE with 20–100 participants?
mcq.why: Phase 1: safety and dosage, 20–100 participants (healthy or with the condition), several months, ~70% progress. Phase 2 is efficacy and side effects in several hundred participants.

mcq.q: Which body assesses the science, safety and appropriateness of a proposed trial DESIGN in NZ?
mcq.why: SCOTT — the Standing Committee on Therapeutic Trials. Medsafe reviews preclinical studies, PK/PD, chemical stability and quality; HDEC checks ethical compliance.

mcq.q: An advertisement that mentions only the drug name, without saying what it treats, is a:
mcq.why: Reminder ads mention the drug name only, without stating what it treats. Health-seeking ads educate about a condition; direct-to-consumer ads promote a specific branded prescription medicine.

mcq.q: Which drug was originally developed for blood pressure and is now used as a topical hair-restoring agent?
mcq.why: Minoxidil was originally developed for blood pressure. Sildenafil was developed for angina and high blood pressure and is now used for impotence; penicillin was discovered from a mould.

mcq.q: Which statement about a nurse and medicine advertising is CORRECT?
options: Advertising rules apply only to printed media
Verbal recommendation of a brand can count as advertising
Nurses are exempt from all advertising rules
Advertising unapproved medicines to health professionals is permitted
mcq.why: Advertising is defined broadly and includes verbal advertising, so praising one brand over another is caught. The rules apply across all media, and advertising unapproved medicines is prohibited even to health professionals.

mcq.q: Placebo use in a trial is ethically acceptable when:
options: No proven treatment exists, or it is necessary for methodology without causing serious harm
mcq.why: Placebo use is problematic if recipients risk harm or worsening of their condition; it is acceptable when no proven treatment exists, or where necessary for methodology without causing serious harm.

topics.name: Anaphylaxis & the ASCIA Plan
topics.chapters: Module 8 · ASCIA Action Plan for Anaphylaxis (2026)

recall.q: List the six steps of the ASCIA anaphylaxis action plan, in order.
recall.src: ASCIA Action Plan for Anaphylaxis (2026), p.1
a: 1. Lay the person FLAT — do NOT allow them to stand or walk.
2. Give the adrenaline device.
3. Phone ambulance — 111 (NZ).
4. Phone family/emergency contact.
5. Further adrenaline may be given if no response after 5 minutes.
6. Transfer the person to hospital for at least 4 hours of observation.

recall.q: What are the positioning rules in step 1, including the three exceptions?
recall.src: ASCIA Action Plan for Anaphylaxis (2026), p.1
a: Lay the person flat — do NOT allow them to stand or walk.
If unconscious or pregnant, place in the recovery position — on the left side if pregnant.
If breathing is difficult, allow them to sit with legs outstretched.
Hold young children flat, not upright.

recall.q: Name the seven signs of anaphylaxis on the ASCIA plan.
recall.src: ASCIA Action Plan for Anaphylaxis (2026), p.1
a: Difficult or noisy breathing.
Swelling or tightness in the throat.
Difficulty talking or hoarse voice.
Wheeze or persistent cough.
Persistent dizziness or collapse.
Pale and floppy (young children).
Swelling of the tongue.

recall.q: Name the signs and the actions for a mild to moderate allergic reaction.
recall.src: ASCIA Action Plan for Anaphylaxis (2026), p.1
a: SIGNS: swelling of lips, face and eyes; hives or welts; tingling mouth.
Abdominal pain and vomiting — but these are signs of ANAPHYLAXIS for insect allergy.
ACTIONS: stay with the person, call for help.
Locate the adrenaline (epinephrine) device.
Give an antihistamine; phone family/emergency contact.
Insect allergy — flick out the sting if visible. Tick allergy — seek medical help, or freeze the tick and let it drop off.

recall.q: A person with known asthma and food allergy has sudden breathing difficulty. What is given first, and why does this matter?
recall.src: ASCIA Action Plan for Anaphylaxis (2026), p.1
a: ALWAYS give the adrenaline device FIRST, then the asthma reliever puffer.

This applies to someone with known asthma and allergy to food, insects or medication who may have been exposed to the allergen, and has sudden breathing difficulty — including wheeze, persistent cough or hoarse voice.
It matters because anaphylaxis can occur WITHOUT skin symptoms, and mild to moderate reactions may not always occur before anaphylaxis.
The plan's overriding rule: IF IN DOUBT, GIVE THE ADRENALINE DEVICE.

recall.q: When should CPR be commenced, and what should be done if a device is accidentally activated?
recall.src: ASCIA Action Plan for Anaphylaxis (2026), p.1
a: Commence CPR at any time if the person is unresponsive or not breathing normally.
If the device is accidentally injected or activated, use another adrenaline device if available.
If adrenaline is accidentally injected, contact the local poisons information centre.

mcq.q: What is step 1 of the ASCIA anaphylaxis action plan?
mcq.why: Step 1 is to lay the person flat and NOT allow them to stand or walk. The adrenaline device is step 2, and phoning the ambulance is step 3.
mcq.src: ASCIA Action Plan for Anaphylaxis (2026), p.1

mcq.q: A person with known asthma and a food allergy has sudden wheeze after a suspected exposure. You should give:
options: The asthma reliever puffer first, then adrenaline
The adrenaline device first, then the asthma reliever puffer
mcq.why: "ALWAYS GIVE ADRENALINE DEVICE FIRST, then asthma reliever puffer." Anaphylaxis can occur without skin symptoms, so waiting for a rash is not safe.
mcq.src: ASCIA Action Plan for Anaphylaxis (2026), p.1

mcq.q: After giving adrenaline with no response, how long before further adrenaline may be given?
mcq.why: Step 5 of the plan: further adrenaline may be given if there is no response after 5 minutes. Step 6 is transfer to hospital for at least 4 hours of observation.
mcq.src: ASCIA Action Plan for Anaphylaxis (2026), p.1

mcq.q: A pregnant person is unconscious from anaphylaxis. They should be placed:
options: In the recovery position on the left side
Flat on their back with legs raised
mcq.why: If unconscious or pregnant, place in the recovery position — on the LEFT side if pregnant.
mcq.src: ASCIA Action Plan for Anaphylaxis (2026), p.1

mcq.q: Abdominal pain and vomiting are signs of ANAPHYLAXIS (rather than a mild-to-moderate reaction) in which situation?
mcq.why: The plan annotates abdominal pain and vomiting with "these are signs of anaphylaxis for insect allergy" in both columns.
mcq.src: ASCIA Action Plan for Anaphylaxis (2026), p.1
